fundamental.thesis: Reliance is a conglomerate with four main businesses: oil refining and chemicals (O2C), Jio telecom (now listed separately as JPL), retail (RRVL) and new energy. Per the sector card it should be valued business by business (sum of the parts), not as a pure oil company. In Q2FY27 gross revenue was a record ₹362,268 cr, up 27.8% YoY, and PAT was ₹29,550 cr, up 33.8% YoY. Revenue growth has picked up from about -8.5% in FY26 to +24.5% in Q1 and +27.8% in Q2, and PAT margin improved from 6.8% in Q1 to 8.2%. However, much of this growth came from O2C, whose EBITDA rose 67.9% because fuel margins spiked on Middle East supply disruption. Retail PAT fell 24.3% and JioStar PAT fell 13.2%, and only Jio is growing steadily (revenue +11.4%, monthly ARPU ₹218.8). We have no sum-of-the-parts data, so as a fallback we used EV/EBITDA of 12.2x and trailing P/E of 21.7x. These look expensive next to the PSU energy peers (median 9.2x P/E, 6.1x EV/EBITDA), but those peers are policy-priced single businesses and not a fair yardstick for a conglomerate. With forward P/E at 18.0x, earnings estimates raised 15-21% over the last 30 days and the price near its 52-week low, we grade valuation fair, not expensive. The biggest risk is that record O2C margins are a temporary geopolitical windfall while retail and media are shrinking, at a time when ROE is only 9.1% and finance costs are up 24.2%.

fundamental.thesis: HDFC Bank is India's largest private-sector bank, with ₹33.2L cr of deposits, ₹33.2L cr of advances and 9,706 branches, and its asset quality is very clean: GNPA is 1.11%, down from 1.15% at FY26-end, net NPA is 0.37% and credit cost is 44 bps. On volume, Q2FY27 deposits grew +18.8% YoY and advances grew +16.3%, but profitability is moving the wrong way. Management calls the 3.32% NIM a cycle low, ROA has fallen from 1.9% in FY26 to 1.48% in H1FY27, and H1 PAT of ₹35,869 cr is down -10.2% YoY on revenue down -4.1%, a 14.3% PAT margin. The ₹1,950 cr Q2 PAT figure (+12.7%) looks like an extraction error, and 30-day and 90-day FY EPS estimates have both been cut 5.6%. Using the lender yardstick of P/B against ROE, 1.98x book on a 13.8% TTM ROE (12.1% in H1) is fair in absolute terms, but it ranks P79 among bank peers on P/B even though P/E sits at the peer median of 16.8x. The stock is at 8.6% of its 52-week range, which helps the entry but does not make it cheap. The biggest risk is an abrupt leadership change: a new MD/CEO effective immediately and the Deputy MD retiring by December. This comes with a loan-to-deposit ratio near 100%, LCR tight at 113%, and a 25 bps October rate hike that management expects to reprice the 70% floating book upward, which conflicts with the sector card's easing-cycle prior.

fundamental.thesis: TCS is India's largest IT services company (₹8L cr market cap, near-debt-free with filing-reported D/E 0.099 and ROE 51%), serving global clients across BFSI (39.1% of revenue), Manufacturing, and Consumer verticals with dominant scale and 12-year consecutive top-ranked customer satisfaction. Revenue re-accelerated sharply in H1 FY27 to ₹1,45,463 cr (+12.6% YoY, with Q1FY27 at +13.9%), up from a sluggish +4.6% in FY26, and PAT margins expanded from 15.9% in Q3FY26 to 18.8% in H1 FY27 — but the critical flag is that FY26 constant-currency growth was -2.4%, meaning the INR headline re-acceleration is substantially FX-tailwind-driven (INR/USD ~94.96 vs ~84 in FY26) rather than evidence of genuine organic demand recovery; EBITDA margins have also contracted from 28.7% to 27.2%, and deferred revenue declined ₹1,092 cr QoQ, both pointing to margin and pipeline softening beneath the headline beat. At 16.3× trailing P/E — a 33.7% discount to the IT sector peer median of 24.7× and cheapest in sector on forward P/E at 13.4× — TCS screens unambiguously cheap versus both sector peers and the benchmark range of 22–30×, with a pristine balance sheet (CFO/PAT 0.94×, FCF ₹23,768 cr in H1) providing a durable floor; the P/E yardstick is used here as primary per the asset-light IT services model, and EV/EBITDA at 11.1× (P17 in sector vs median 14.7×) corroborates the cheap read. The central risk is AI-led productivity deflation continuing to compress legacy T&M revenues in constant-currency terms: if INR stabilises from current weakness, CC growth likely reverts to near-zero or negative, the INR acceleration collapses, and the re-rating catalyst disappears, leaving TCS cheap but with no near-term earnings growth to close the discount.

Bharti Airtel is the number-two player in India's repaired 2.5-player mobile oligopoly, with growing broadband, enterprise and Africa businesses on top. The Q2 FY27 trend row shows revenue of ₹6,088 cr (+16.7% YoY) and PAT of ₹889 cr (+30.8% YoY, 14.6% margin). That figure is far too small for consolidated Airtel and does not match the ₹21,097 cr Q4 FY26 row or the ₹211,000 cr FY26 row, so the 'decelerating/contracting' trajectory flags compare different reporting entities and should not be trusted. The cleaner signal is the sector KPIs: mobile ARPU rose to ₹271 (+5.9% YoY, up from ₹257 in Q4 FY26), the customer base grew 11.1% to 692.6 mn, net debt/EBITDA is 1.18x and ROCE is 22.7%, all consistent with the tariff-repair and deleveraging story. Using EV/EBITDA, the yardstick the telecom card names, the stock trades at 10.54x, inside the 9–12x India-mobile norm and at P12 of the broad market, so it grades fair rather than cheap despite a 40.7x trailing P/E. Forward P/E of 21.6x implies earnings growth is expected, and the price sits at 15% of its 52-week range, a reasonable entry if ARPU keeps compounding. The main risk is that ARPU growth of about 6% is modest without a fresh tariff hike, and slight FY-EPS cuts (-0.6% over 30 and 90 days) against a 32-of-34 buy rating mix leave room for disappointment.

In Q2FY27, net total income grew 23% YoY to ₹15,974 cr and PAT grew 29% to ₹6,367 cr, while AUM growth picked up from 22.4% (Q4FY26) to 24% (Q1) to 26%, and GNPA improved to 1.06% from 1.24% a year ago. Note that the trend table's Q1FY27 and H1 'revenue' rows appear to use total income rather than net income, so I rely on the like-for-like Q2 net-income figures. Using the sector card's lender yardstick of P/B against ROE, the stock trades at 4.93x book for a 17.9% TTM ROE (20.6% annualised in Q2), the most expensive P/B among its 10 credit-services peers (P100, +62% vs the 3.0x median) and P89 on P/E at 29.6x, so it is expensive even after allowing a quality premium. The 18.3x forward P/E and the 62% dividend yield look like data errors and are not relied on. The biggest risk is that management itself guides to modest NIM moderation with up to two more repo hikes to 6%, which turns the NBFC rate tailwind into a headwind. Stage 2 and 3 assets have also risen to 2.02% from 1.87%, and the ₹17,500 cr QIP plus promoter warrants will dilute ROE in the near term.

Mahindra & Mahindra is India's SUV leader (24.4% auto revenue market share, 32.3% eSUV share) and the dominant tractor maker (43.4% farm volume share), with financial services, Tech Mahindra and real estate arms inside the consolidated numbers. In Q2FY27 consolidated revenue rose +25.0% YoY to ₹57,553 cr and PAT rose +25.0% to ₹4,588 cr, so top-line growth is holding steady around +25–28%; however, PAT margin has slipped from 10.3% in Q1FY27 to 8.0%, and management cut the full-year tractor outlook from +5% to flattish after a weak monsoon. On valuation, using P/E plus EV/EBITDA as the yardstick for a capital-intensive OEM, the trailing P/E of 19.5× sits at the low end of the 18–30× OEM range and 28% below the peer median of 27.1×, while EV/EBITDA of 10.7× is 41% below the peer median of 18.3×; the stock also trades near its 52-week low, so the grade is cheap. Part of this discount is reasonable for a conglomerate structure, and the biggest risk is margin squeeze: commodity inflation is outrunning +5% price hikes in auto while rural and farm demand weakens, and sell-side estimates have been trimmed 2.5% over 90 days.

fundamental.thesis: Kotak Mahindra Bank is one of India's largest private-sector banks, with a strong capital base (CET1 22.1%) and growing wealth and asset-management arms (customer AUM ₹8.14L cr, +8% YoY). Profit growth has picked up sharply: consolidated PAT rose 26.3% YoY to ₹5,645 cr in Q2FY27, up from +23.0% in Q1FY27 and +5.0% in Q3FY26, and standalone NII rose 16% to ₹8,459 cr. Asset quality has improved steadily, with GNPA falling from 1.39% to 1.04% over five periods and slippages down 24%, but this quarter's growth comes partly off a weak base (Q2FY26 PAT was -2.7%), and NIM fell 23bps YoY to 4.31% as costlier FCNR(B) deposits came in. On the bank yardstick (P/B plus ROE, not P/E), a P/B of 2.08x against an ROE of only 11.4-11.7% is fair, not cheap; it sits at the 86th percentile among bank peers on both P/B and forward P/E (13.6x), so it already carries a premium that its current ROE does not clearly earn. The biggest risk is margin squeeze: falling NIM, CASA slipping from 42.3% to 41.8%, a 4.52% cost of funds and an 8.1% cut to next-FY EPS estimates while 32 of 37 analysts still rate it a buy, a pattern that often comes before a re-rating lower.

Maruti Suzuki is India's largest passenger-car maker and also India's top EV exporter, having crossed 50,000 EV exports. The only usable figures are for H1 FY27: revenue of ₹1,00,575 cr (+31.0% YoY) lines up with 13.79 lakh wholesale units at an average selling price of about ₹7.29 lakh, but PAT fell 18.3% to ₹5,767 cr and PAT margin is just 5.7%, so sales are growing while profits shrink. The 1H FY26, FY26 and Q3FY26 rows look like Suzuki Motor Corporation parent or mixed-entity data and were not used, and the Q2 FY27 results filed on 2026-10-27 have not yet been extracted. On valuation, using P/E with EV/EBITDA as a cross-check, the stock trades at 27.6x trailing earnings, inside the 18–30x range for auto makers and at the peer median (P60 on P/E, P50 on EV/EBITDA at 18.3x), so it is fair; trading at 19.5% of its 52-week range and a forward P/E of 20.8x both point to a better entry, provided earnings recover. The main risk is that the volume and price boost from the GST cut is not reaching the bottom line because of cost pressure or price discounting.

fundamental.thesis: Axis Bank is India's third-largest private-sector bank, with a large corporate and wholesale book, a growing retail franchise and a consolidated life-insurance associate (Axis Max Life). In Q2FY27, total income rose 14.8% YoY to ₹45,674 cr and PAT rose 39.4% to ₹7,705 cr. Revenue growth has picked up from about +4% (H1FY26) to +7% (Q1FY27) to +15%, and loan growth has risen from 11.9% to 19.3%, but the PAT jump is flattered by a weak Q2FY26 base (₹5,528 cr), and the PAT margin slipped from 17.7% in Q1 to 16.9%. On the lender yardstick from the sector card (P/B against sustainable ROE), a P/B of 1.83x for a TTM ROE of 13.2% is fair: it is above the peer median of 1.5x (P64), while trailing P/E of 15.0x is about 11% below peers (P43). That fits a bank whose asset quality has improved (GNPA down from 1.46% to 1.23%) but whose returns are only moderate. The biggest risk is that loans are now growing faster than deposits: the loan-to-deposit ratio is a stretched 98.7%, credit cost has risen from 0.20% to 0.72%, and provision coverage is slipping (70.5% to 70.0%). Together these point to future funding-cost and NIM pressure, and the extracted NIM readings (3.42% in Q1 vs 2.32% in Q2) conflict too much to confirm the NIM recovery the sector card expects.

The weak 6.5% PAT margin and the drop in EBITDA per tonne from ₹1,214 in Q1 mostly reflect the monsoon quarter, though fuel (+14%) and packing-bag (+30%) costs are rising with crude. The preferred cement yardstick, EV/EBITDA, was unavailable, so I graded on peers: a trailing P/E of 39.6x sits near the Materials peer median of 37.3x (P53) and the forward P/E is 25.1x, which makes it fair, but a P/B of 4.5x against a 10.6% ROE is rich, and the biggest risk is sell-side FY EPS estimates being cut 11–13% over 90 days while 33 of 37 analysts still rate it a buy, a classic pre-derating pattern.

fundamental.thesis: HCL Technologies is India's #3 IT services company with a differentiated HCLSoftware products arm, competing globally in cloud, AI, and enterprise services — a revenue-mix edge over pure-play peers TCS and Infosys that should sustain margin resilience through the sector's AI-reset cycle. Using P/E as the primary IT yardstick (per the sector card), a trailing P/E of 19× sits 14% below the sector floor of 22× and at a 23% discount to the peer median of 24.7× (P38 in sector), screening cheap; forward P/E of 14.4× below trailing implies earnings growth is priced in, but the stock at just 7.5% of its 52-week range with sell-side mean targets -8% below market price signals the market is discounting risks not yet visible in Q1 data. The unresolved critical risk is that Q2FY27 results (filed 2026-10-12, Sep quarter) are not yet extracted — this analysis is one quarter stale precisely when the stock has significantly de-rated, and the unread filing likely contains the catalyst for that weakness.

Titan is India's largest organised jewellery retailer (Tanishq, CaratLane, about 8.5% organised share), with fast-growing watches and eyecare businesses and roughly 3,758 stores. Consolidated revenue grew 25.1% YoY in Q2FY27 to ₹20,533 cr, up from roughly +13% in Q1 (implied by H1 growth of +19.1% to ₹41,970 cr), with jewellery SSSG of 15% and studded mix rising to 35%. H1 PAT of ₹4,170 cr (+88.6%, 9.9% margin) is inflated by about ₹536 cr of one-time customs-duty benefits and a ₹671 cr Damas option-liability reduction; management puts normalised EBIT growth nearer 20–27%. On valuation, the sector card's premium-retail yardstick (60–100x is normal for this group, judged alongside SSSG and unit economics) makes trailing P/E of 74.3x and forward P/E of 49.4x look fair. Against peers it looks rich: P/E is at P76 and EV/EBITDA of 48.1x is at P94, so I grade it fair at the top end of fair. The main risk is that growth now comes from bigger ticket sizes rather than more buyers (buyer growth was flat YoY), while H1 cash flow was sharply negative (FCF ₹-11,585 cr) from inventory build, leaving it exposed to a gold-price or demand reset.

fundamental.thesis: ONGC is India's largest upstream oil and gas producer, a state-run company whose earnings rise with crude prices, and that upside is limited by government policy such as windfall taxes. The indexed trend table is stale and only runs to FY26, when revenue fell 3.9% to ₹132,508 cr and PAT fell 7.6% to ₹32,894 cr, continuing a steady decline. The biggest risk is that the rebound comes from elevated crude caused by the West Asia conflict, not from higher volumes, so a crude pullback or a new windfall levy could reverse it quickly.

The jump in PAT margin from 5.6–6.5% to 13–15% looks partly like a change in reporting basis (owners' share vs consolidated), so I treat the margin trend with caution. On valuation I used P/B against ROE, the lender yardstick from the sector card, along with the holding-company view: P/B of 3.53x on 14.6% ROE sits at the 73rd percentile of peers and is +75% above the sector median. Trailing P/E is 28.2x but forward P/E is 18.7x, and the stock is at only 21% of its 52-week range, so overall valuation is fair rather than cheap, given the usual holding-company discount. The main risk is that lending growth is slowing while the insurance businesses weaken: General insurance's combined ratio rose to 104.5% (PAT -19%), life retail premium growth is only 5%, and next-year earnings estimates have been cut 3.0–3.5% even though most analysts still rate it a buy.

Profit has moved the opposite way: Q2FY27 PAT fell 26.6% YoY (Q1 was -35.9%), and EBITDA margin compressed from 32.9% to 24.0%. Depreciation doubled, interest costs rose 85% and medtech runs a -29% segment margin, all signs of a costly investment and acquisition cycle. Note that the Q2 row appears to carry a 10x unit error (₹791 cr revenue against an H1 of ₹15,927 cr), so the growth and margin ratios are usable but the absolute figures are not. On valuation, using P/E and EV/EBITDA against peers as the yardstick, trailing P/E of 21.7x looks cheap against the 28–40x pharma range and P8 among peers. That trailing number is flattered by peak FY26 US earnings, though: forward P/E of 23.3x (P38) sits above trailing, EV/EBITDA of 16.1x is only P31, and the stock is at 90% of its 52-week range, so overall it grades fair rather than a bargain. The biggest risk is that US revenue, already -5.7% in Q4 FY26 and guided only to single-digit growth, slips further, through tariff review of generics or the five FDA observations at Moraiya, while margins are still compressing. FY-EPS estimates are already being cut (-3.7% over 90 days).

fundamental.thesis: Adani Green Energy is India's largest renewable power producer. It runs 20,763 MW of operating capacity, up 24% YoY, with the 30 GW Khavda park at its core, and it sells power under 25-year fixed-tariff contracts. In H1 FY27, revenue rose 27.6% YoY to ₹8,689 cr and PAT rose 17.8% to ₹1,730 cr, a 19.9% margin. H1 minus Q1 implies Q2 revenue of about ₹4,258 cr, faster than Q1's +16.6%, but Q2 PAT margin of about 17.5% is below Q1's 22.2%. The 'expanding margin' signal compares half-year, full-year and nine-month figures, so it is not like-for-like and overstates the improvement. This is a capital-intensive business, so I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, and on that basis it is expensive. EV/EBITDA is 31.8x against a utilities peer median of 11.6x, the highest in the group. Price-to-book is 12.7x while ROE is only 7.6%, and the stock sits at 93.6% of its 52-week range. Sell-side earnings estimates have been cut 14.5% over 90 days even though 9 of 10 analysts still rate it a buy, a pattern that often comes before a re-rating lower. The main risk is the balance sheet: net debt is 5.6x run-rate EBITDA, gross debt is ₹1.12 lakh cr and H1 free cash flow was -₹7,141 cr, so the equity depends on capacity coming online on time and on cheap refinancing. That is happening while US yields are at 5% and the rupee is weakening.

fundamental.thesis: GAIL is India's largest gas transmission and marketing company. Gas marketing produced about 56% of segment profit in H1 (₹7,131 cr), regulated pipelines added ₹3,964 cr at a 58% margin, and petrochemicals lost ₹168 cr. Growth was very strong in H1 FY27: revenue rose 24.7% to ₹88,651 cr and PAT rose 115% to ₹9,395 cr. Q2 looks even faster, with implied revenue of about ₹47,300 cr (roughly +33% YoY, against +16.7% in Q1). By the press-release figures, Q2 revenue was ₹45,924 cr and PAT ₹4,650 cr, a margin of about 10.1%, down from 11.3% in Q1. The pre-computed trend signals mix half-year and quarter periods, so I did not rely on them. Using enterprise value to operating profit (EV/EBITDA) plus dividend yield, as the sector card advises for a volume and tariff business, valuation is fair. EV/EBITDA is 11.6x, exactly the peer median, and trailing P/E is 14.65x, at the peer median and just above the 8–14x energy range. P/B is 1.26x against an annualised H1 ROE of about 19%, which looks attractive. The forward P/E of 9.5x depends on FY27 estimates that analysts raised 28% in 30 days while trimming next-year estimates by 3.5%. The biggest risk is that the doubling of profit comes mostly from gas-marketing spreads, which swing with LNG prices and are not structural. That makes FY27 look like a peak year. The newly started Mangalore PTA plant (purified terephthalic acid, a petrochemical) also adds exposure to a segment that is currently losing money.

In Q2 FY27, total income rose 5.4% YoY to ₹38,185 cr and net profit rose 12.8% to ₹5,532 cr; asset quality keeps improving, with Gross NPA down from 3.19% to 2.95% to 2.55%, Net NPA at 0.25%, slippage at 0.77% and provision coverage at 97%, though the revenue trend is noisy because one period row looks inconsistent. Using the lender yardstick of price-to-book against ROE, the stock trades at 0.83x book against a 13% TTM ROE (17.3% in the latest quarter), which is about 44% below the regional-bank median P/B of 1.5x and in the bottom 15% of peers, so it grades as cheap; the trailing P/E of 6.75x is consistent with that but is not the main yardstick. The main concern is funding: cost of deposits rose from 2.50% to 2.74% YoY, CASA slipped from 37.0% to 36.6%, domestic deposits grew only 9.5% against 12.5% domestic loan growth, and treasury income fell 57%, all of which could cap the 2.6–2.7% margin guidance.

fundamental.thesis: IDFC First Bank is a mid-sized private bank with a retail-heavy loan book and a strong deposit franchise (CASA 48.4%), now scaling fast after years of rebuilding profitability. In Q2FY27, PAT was ₹1,045 cr, up 196.5% YoY off a depressed base and above ₹1,000 cr for a second straight quarter. Loans grew 30.1% YoY (22.2% excluding FCNR(B)-backed loans, up from 20.6% in Q1), deposits grew 25.9%, and asset quality kept improving: net NPA fell from 0.48% to 0.44% to 0.40%, and gross NPA was 1.32% vs 1.61% at FY26-end. Valuation is graded on P/B plus ROE, as the sector card requires for lenders, not on trailing P/E: P/B is 1.31x (P36 among peers, 11% below the 1.5x median) against annualised ROE of only 10.6%, which is below the 12% bar for 'cheap', so the stock is fair. The 38x trailing P/E is distorted by weak FY26 earnings (PAT ₹1,611 cr), and the 11x forward P/E sits exactly at the peer median. The main risk is that rapid growth is outpacing the bank's profitability engine: CASA slipped from 50.8% to 48.4% and NIM was diluted by FCNR(B) funding, Q2 ROA fell to 0.93% from 1.06%, and capital adequacy (CAR) dropped to 15.05% from 15.6% while the loan book grows about 30%.

fundamental.thesis: Indian Hotels (IHCL) runs India's largest hotel chain, with Taj and other brands across 670 hotels including 280 in the pipeline. It earns more and more from asset-light management fees, which grew 25% YoY in Q2, and it is still early in a RevPAR (revenue per available room) upcycle, up 25% YoY in Q2 and 28% for full-service hotels. Q2FY27 revenue rose 21.0% YoY to ₹2,566 cr, up from +14.6% in Q1FY27. PAT rose 23.0% to ₹349 cr. Management raised full-year revenue guidance from 12-14% to 15-17%, and H1 cash conversion was strong (CFO/PAT 1.27x, FCF ₹546 cr). The 'contracting' margin signal mostly reflects comparing a seasonally weak Q2 against full-year figures: on a same-quarter basis the EBITDA margin (30.7%) and PAT margin (13.6%) are roughly flat to slightly up YoY. On valuation, hotels are capital-intensive, so I used EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick. At 28.2x, IHCL sits around the 61st percentile of its sector, with a trailing P/E of 44.5x (P59) and a forward P/E of 35.6x. That is fair, not cheap, for 20%+ earnings growth, and the stock sits at 38.5% of its 52-week range. Note that the snapshot's 49% dividend yield and 18.99 debt/equity look like data-unit errors, given ₹4,369 cr of gross cash. The biggest risk is that a premium-multiple discretionary stock gets de-rated in a risk-off market with crude above $100, which could squeeze travel and MICE (meetings, incentives, conferences and events) demand even while operating numbers stay strong.

Positives exist but did not lift the stock: premiumisation rose to 18.6%, ROCE is 121%, and gross margin is 69.7%. Weakness in Palmolive personal care is an admitted concern.
Data gaps lower confidence: no FinBERT score, sector flow is neutral (FMCG trails the benchmark by 1.1% over 5 days), and FMCG faces a mild macro headwind in a risk-on regime.

technical.setup: Bounce in a long-term downtrend: price has rallied off its lows back up to the 50-day average (about ₹1,742) and is testing it, with MACD momentum turning up, but the 50-day sits below the 200-day, price is 10% under the 200-day, and the stock is lagging both Nifty and its FMCG peers.

trader.reasoning: The business is high quality and the valuation is only fair: sales are growing about 12%, but profit growth has slowed to 4% because heavy ad spending is squeezing margins. The market sold the stock off after Q2 results, and sentiment is bearish. The chart shows only a bounce up to the 50-day average inside a longer downtrend, with the stock lagging Nifty and its FMCG peers. FMCG is underweight in today's risk-on macro view, the analysts disagree, and cash is limited, so there is no case for opening a new position. We will revisit if profit growth recovers or the price reclaims its 200-day average.

fundamental.thesis: Colgate-Palmolive India is the dominant oral-care franchise, with the number one toothpaste brand at roughly three times the size of the second player, 69-70% gross margins and an 81.6% ROE. Revenue growth has picked up from flat in FY26 to +9.0% in Q4FY26 and about +12% for the last two quarters, reaching Rs 1,706 cr (+12.4% YoY) in Q2FY27 on high-single-digit toothpaste volume growth, but PAT growth slowed from +10.6% to +4.3% (Rs 342 cr). PAT margin fell from 22.3% to 20.0% and EBITDA margin from 32.2% to 29.0% because ad spend rose 39.8% YoY to 18.4% of sales, while gross margin held flat. On the FMCG yardstick of P/E cross-checked with EV/EBITDA, trailing P/E of 41.1x sits at the low end of the 40-60x sector band and 6% below the peer median of 43.8x (P40), EV/EBITDA of 28.3x is at P20, and forward P/E of 34.1x implies earnings growth, so the stock grades fair with the price at 33% of its 52-week range. The main risk is that the heavy ad spending does not turn into lasting volume and premium-mix gains, leaving profit growth stuck in low single digits while revenue grows double digits.

drivers: News reports a weak Q2: 'Berger Paints hopes for gloss back on volume and margin after pale Q2' (one story syndicated across 4 headlines), citing volume and margin pressure
Q2 seems to have missed management's Q1FY27 call that Q2 would be 'possibly slightly better than Q1'. That guidance is 99 days old (stale) and was only neutral (reiterated)
Market reaction to the Nov-5 results was in-line but negative: -1.4% after 1 day, widening to -2.9% after 2 days
Sector flow is neutral (Materials +0.56% vs benchmark), so no tailwind offsets the stock-specific weakness

technical.setup: Range-bound consolidation with no real trend (ADX 18.3): price sits between SMA50 support near 468 and SMA200 resistance near 480. Long-term structure is still a death-cross and the stock is clearly lagging both the Nifty and its paint/materials peers. A mildly positive MACD is not enough to call a breakout.

trader.reasoning: Revenue growth is picking up (about +13% in Q2), but profitability is slipping. Q2 operating profit grew only about 5%, margins fell sharply from Q1 and cash conversion was weak, while a fair-to-full valuation (about 51x trailing P/E) leaves no cushion if costs keep rising and Birla Opus keeps competing hard. Sentiment is bearish after a pale Q2 that the market sold off. The chart is trendless (ADX 18) and stuck between SMA50 support near 468 and SMA200 resistance near 480, with the long-term death-cross intact, so no pillar supports a new entry. We hold no position here, so the bearish tilt means staying out; we would revisit on evidence that margins have stabilised or on a clean move above the 200-day average.

fundamental.thesis: Berger Paints is India's number-two decorative paints maker, with growing industrial, construction-chemical and international businesses, and it says its market share stayed stable through Q2 even as Birla Opus pushes into the market. Revenue growth has sped up from +0.4% YoY in Q3FY26 to +6.7% in Q4FY26, +12.0% in Q1FY27 and +13.2% in Q2FY27. H1FY27 revenue was ₹6,784 cr (+12.5%) and PAT ₹622 cr (+19.3%). Margins are moving the other way: subtracting Q1 from H1 gives Q2 revenue of about ₹3,200 cr and PAT of about ₹217 cr, a PAT margin near 6.8% against 11.3% in Q1. Q2 operating profit grew only 5.2% and standalone EBITDA margin fell 4.4pp because of sharp raw-material inflation and higher ad spend. Because paints are a consumer franchise, I graded valuation on P/E against the sector card's 30–60× band rather than against steel and metals stocks: a trailing P/E of 50.9× (38.7× forward) is fair, though top quartile within Materials (P87), and it sits below the priciest peers ASIANPAINT and PIDILITIND. The 52-week position is mid-range at 48%. The biggest risk is that management sees no easing in input costs and is relying on further price increases from November, while a new entrant makes it harder to pass costs on. Cash conversion is also very weak, with H1 CFO/PAT at 0.23x and free cash flow of -₹82 cr.

technical.setup: Sharp rebound breakout to the upper Bollinger band (%B 0.96) on strong bullish MACD, ADX 34 and accumulation volume, but it is still inside a long-term downtrend: price is 7% below the 200-day average, SMA50 sits below SMA200, and the stock is lagging Nifty. That makes it an extended counter-trend rally, not a pullback entry, and the current regime does not reward chasing breakouts.

trader.reasoning: The business is strong: about 30% ROE, profit up 43% YoY, a cheap P/E against peers, and a good market reaction to the Oct-31 results. But adding now would mean chasing an extended counter-trend rally (%B 0.96, still below the 200-day average) while three risks build: gold has fallen to about $3,883, reported gross NPA has jumped to about 2.3%, and a GST search was disclosed on 2-Nov. The technical analyst rates it hold, and fundamental data quality is only partial. Keep the 2.2% position (+13.8% unrealised, short-term gain of about ₹2,460, so selling now would cost roughly ₹490 in STCG) with a stop near the ₹2,703 support, and consider adding only on a pullback to that support if credit quality stabilises.

fundamental.thesis: Muthoot Finance is India's largest gold-loan NBFC, with very high profitability: annualised ROE of about 29% and ROA of about 5.4% in H1 FY27, and NIM of 10.4% in Q1 FY27. Growth is strong but slowing. Q1 FY27 revenue was Rs 8,695 cr (+34.5% YoY) and PAT was Rs 2,825 cr (+43.1% YoY), and AUM growth has eased from about 50% to 43% YoY over the last four periods. PAT margin has slipped from 36.2% in 9M FY26 to 32.5% in Q1 FY27; H1 FY27 PAT of Rs 6,046 cr implies Q2 PAT of about Rs 3,221 cr, but YoY growth for Q2 cannot be computed from the data given. Using the lender yardstick (P/B against sustainable ROE), P/B of 3.0x sits exactly at the peer median (P44) while ROE of about 30% is well above most peers, and trailing P/E of 11.2x is in the cheapest quartile of peers (P22, 44% below the 20.1x median), so the stock is fair, leaning cheap. The biggest risk is that this ROE is boosted by a historically high gold price, now at $4,075/oz and falling. On top of that come a reported gross NPA jump from 0.14% to about 2.3%, a CGST Section 67 tax search disclosed on 2026-11-02, and several data inconsistencies.

Aurobindo Pharma is one of India's largest export-led generics makers: 92% of revenue comes from overseas, with the US at 44% and Europe at 31%, backed by 747 cumulative US FDA final approvals and a net cash position of $189M. Revenue growth has sped up from +8.4% YoY in Q3FY26 and +6.1% for FY26 to +16.3% in Q1FY27 and +23.9% in Q2FY27 (₹10,263 cr), and Q2 PAT rose 32.5% to ₹1,124 cr. PAT margin improved to 11.0% from 10.4–10.5%, though EBITDA margin slipped from 23.0% in Q1 to 21.0% in Q2, and the jump comes right after a quarter where US revenue fell 13%, so part of it may be one-offs or inorganic and should not yet be treated as run-rate. On valuation, using P/E and EV/EBITDA against generic-pharma peers, the stock is cheap: trailing P/E is 24.0x against a peer median of 36.4x and below the sector's 28–40x band, EV/EBITDA is 12.0x (cheapest of 13 peers), and forward P/E of 16.4x signals expected earnings growth, though the price already sits at 85% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is heavy US exposure while the US Commerce review of generics tariffs is pending, plus binary FDA outcomes; Apitoria Unit-2's 'Voluntary Action Indicated' result is benign, but the Lannet classification was not specified.

drivers: News: USFDA gave a subsidiary manufacturing unit an 'OAI' (Official Action Indicated) rating. Headlines say shares 'extend losses' and the stock 'snaps 12-day winning streak'. This is a fresh, high-materiality regulatory hit that came after the results.

Management tone is neutral. FY27 guidance was only reiterated: double-digit growth and EBITDA margins north of 21%. Record Q2 revenue of ₹10,263 Cr (up 24% YoY) and 28% EBITDA growth are real positives, but guidance was not raised.
Earnings reaction was in-line (+1.4% one day after results). The market did not reward the record quarter strongly, so there is little support against the FDA overhang.
Management flagged risks: input and freight cost pressure, China plant still loss-making, and Lannett plant underused. No FinBERT score is available, which leaves a data gap and limits conviction.

technical.setup: Clean, strong uptrend: price is above the 20-, 50- and 200-day averages, the 50-day sits above the 200-day, MACD is positive, ADX is 28.4 and buying volume is building. But the BREAKOUT label comes with the stock stretched near the upper Bollinger band (%B 0.94), RSI at 69.8 and price about 8.7% above the 20-day average, and today's momentum regime says not to rate extended breakouts 'buy'. So wait for a pullback toward the 1,680–1,700 support zone instead of chasing the move.

trader.reasoning: The fundamentals still back holding: good data, a cheap valuation (24x trailing P/E against a 36x peer median, cheapest EV/EBITDA of 13 peers) and strong growth (Q2 revenue +24%, PAT +32.5%). But a fresh USFDA 'OAI' rating at a subsidiary unit has turned sentiment bearish. That conflicts with the fundamental note that Apitoria Unit-2 got a benign 'VAI' and that Lannett's status is unclear, so the true earnings impact is still unresolved. The chart is also extended (RSI 69.8, %B 0.94, about 8.7% above the 20-day average), and the technical view is to wait for a pullback rather than chase. The position is already 4.9% of the portfolio, at the 5% hard per-stock limit, so adding is off the table even though the displayed 9% cap would allow it. Trimming is not justified either: the gain of about ₹4,200 (+10.1%) is short-term and would be taxed at 20%, and the fundamental thesis has not broken. Keep the position with a stop just below the ₹1,682 support and near the ₹1,659 average cost, which protects capital if the FDA issue widens. Revisit if Lannett gets an adverse classification or the US generics tariff review goes against the company.

trader.reasoning: Lupin looks cheap next to its peers, but profits are falling, margins are getting thinner, and management expects margins to ease further, so the low price may reflect lower future earnings rather than a bargain. News sentiment is neutral and offers no support. The chart shows a short bounce running into resistance at the 50-day average inside a longer downtrend, which is not a buy setup. With no position and all three views mixed to lukewarm, staying out is the safer call; a sustained move above about 2035 with stabilising margins would be worth a fresh look.

fundamental.thesis: Lupin is a large Indian generics maker with a broad US business (3rd by prescriptions, about 5% of US generic prescriptions) and a chronic-led India franchise that is growing slightly faster than the market (India Rx +14.4% vs market +14.3%, chronic +19.5% vs +17.2%). Growth has slowed while margins are shrinking: Q2 FY27 revenue of about ₹7,827 cr (derived as H1 ₹16,104 cr minus Q1 ₹8,277 cr) grew +14.0% YoY, down from +32.1% in Q1. Q2 PAT of about ₹1,186 cr (derived) fell roughly 22-25% YoY, and H1 PAT fell 10.9% even as H1 revenue rose 20.9%, as EBITDA margin slipped from 31.5% in FY26 to 29.5% in H1 and to about 25% in Q2, the pharma operating margin fell to 22.9% from 26.5%, and the tax rate rose to 26.7% from 13.4%. On the business-model yardstick for generics (EV/EBITDA cross-checked with P/E), the stock looks cheap: EV/EBITDA is 12.4x (P8 among 13 peers, 42% below the 21.4x median) and trailing P/E is 19.4x, the cheapest in the peer set and below the 28-40x sector band. However, forward P/E of 22.1x is above trailing, and next-year EPS estimates have been cut 4.6% over 90 days, so the market expects earnings to fall from FY26's elevated base. The biggest risk is that FY26's +62% PAT jump included US windfalls that are not repeatable, which would mean the low multiple reflects falling earnings rather than mispricing; the pending US tariff review of generics and ₹5,817 mn of remaining antitrust provisions add further risk.

Page Industries is India's dominant branded innerwear and athleisure company, holding the exclusive Jockey licence (plus Speedo) and running a very asset-light model with about 1,616 exclusive stores, ROE of about 52% and net cash of about ₹445 cr. Revenue growth has picked up over three quarters, from +5.6% in Q3FY26 to +7.9% in Q1FY27 to +11.5% in Q2FY27 (₹1,440 cr vs ₹1,291 cr). Profit has not kept pace: Q2 PAT rose only 4.0% to ₹203 cr, and EBITDA margin fell 134 bps YoY to 20.85%, so the 'PAT margin expanding' signal overstates the quality of the rebound. Cash generation is strong, with H1 FCF of ₹436 cr and CFO/PAT of 2.36x. On valuation, the yardstick used is P/E and EV/EBITDA against peers, given the asset-light franchise. Trailing P/E is 56.2x and forward P/E is 44.9x, versus a mixed peer median of 39.7x (P71) and the card's 60-100x range for premium consumer franchises; EV/EBITDA is 37.0x (P78) and P/B is at P95. That makes the stock fair: a deserved quality premium, but little room for error while FY EPS estimates have been cut about 5% over 90 days. Several snapshot fields look wrong and were not used: the 156% dividend yield, the 18.4 debt/equity (filings show net cash, so this is probably a percentage), the +31.7% target upside (the ₹41,957 mean target is only about 9% above an implied price near ₹38,500), and the garbled FY26/Q4 trend row. The biggest risk is that revenue keeps growing while margins keep shrinking.

trader.reasoning: Page Industries is a high-quality, cash-rich franchise. Revenue growth is picking up, but profit is not keeping pace: Q2 EBITDA margin fell 134 bps and PAT grew only 4%, and the market punished this with a lower-circuit fall. At 45-56x earnings, with EPS estimates being cut, the stock is only fairly valued. On the charts there is no real trend (ADX 18), price sits just above flat 50- and 200-day averages, and the stock is lagging its peers, so there is no pullback-to-support or oversold-reversal entry. With no pillar supporting a buy, a sector underweight, and one share already worth about 3.9% of the portfolio, we stay out. We will revisit if margins stabilise next quarter or price makes a confirmed reversal from support near 35,956.

trader.reasoning: Profit growth is strong, but the stock looks expensive at about 3.6x book. Bad loans got slightly worse and an unresolved data-leak report adds risk, so the fundamentals do not justify paying up. Sentiment is neutral: the market sold the stock 6.8% on results despite the 53% profit rise, because margins slipped and costs grew. The chart shows only a bounce inside a longer downtrend, with price still below falling 50- and 200-day averages and resistance near 990-1000. With no pillar supporting an entry and limited cash in a midcap, we stay out and would revisit on a clean move above 1000 or a cheaper valuation.

fundamental.thesis: AU Small Finance Bank is a mid-sized retail and small-business lender, focused on vehicle loans and mortgages, that is awaiting final approval to become a universal bank. Q2 FY27 revenue growth accelerated from +18.7% to +25.7% YoY to Rs 3,590 cr, and PAT growth rose from +37.0% to +52.9% to Rs 858 cr, but PAT is up only about 3% from Rs 832 cr in Q4 FY26, so an easy prior-year base flatters the YoY figure; the trend table's 'contracting margin' signal looks like an artifact of mixed revenue definitions, as H1 revenue of Rs 12,374 cr is far above the Rs 6,974 cr sum of Q1 and Q2, while NIM slipped from 5.9% to 5.8%, CASA improved from 29.0% to 29.5%, and gross NPA improved from 2.1% to 1.99%. Using P/B plus ROE as the yardstick for lenders, the stock is expensive at 3.64x book against a 1.5x peer median (P100) with FY26 ROE of 14.2%, though the trailing P/E of 27.77x against a 16.8x median is also high, and stronger growth and a peer set that includes low-multiple PSU banks explain only part of the premium. The biggest risks are a slight worsening in net NPA (0.76% to 0.81%) and provision coverage (85% to 83%) at a price that leaves little room for error, plus the potential data leak reported on 2 November, since the bank's reply to the exchange was not available for review; the feed's 10% dividend yield and +24% target upside do not reconcile with the Rs 1 dividend and the roughly Rs 969 price implied by market cap, so neither was relied on.

technical.setup: Breakout in an established uptrend (price above SMA20 > SMA50 > SMA200, MACD positive, rising accumulation volume), but price is well above the upper Bollinger band (%B 1.24) with only early-trend ADX (20.4) and lagging Nifty; under the current momentum-regime rule that rules out chasing a breakout, so the better entry is a pullback toward the SMA20/SMA50 zone.

trader.reasoning: Federal Bank's business is doing well: Q2 FY27 profit rose 45% to a record, bad loans fell to their lowest levels, and the market cheered the October results. Fundamentals and sentiment both lean positive. But the stock is fairly valued at about 1.95x book, which is a premium to peers. It is also stretched technically, trading at 97% of its 52-week range and well above the upper Bollinger band (%B 1.24) on a weak trend (ADX 20). The current regime also says not to chase extended names, so we keep the small 3-share position (up 6.2%, too small for tax to matter) and do not add today. A pullback toward the 341 support or the 20/50-day average zone would be the better entry, provided NIM stops falling from 3.32% and deposit growth catches up with loan growth.

fundamental.thesis: Federal Bank is a mid-sized private-sector bank with a large non-resident (NRI) deposit base. NRE/NRO deposits are about ₹1.19 lakh crore of ₹3.43 lakh crore total deposits, and gross advances have now passed ₹3 lakh crore. In Q2 FY27, PAT hit a record ₹1,386 cr, up 45.1% YoY, and NII grew 26.4% to ₹3,153 cr, faster than loan growth of 21.7%. Net revenue (NII plus other income) was about ₹4,644 cr, up 29.8% YoY. Asset quality improved steadily, with gross NPA falling from 1.83% to 1.32% and net NPA from 0.48% to 0.17% over four quarters. The trend table's 'revenue' row mixes definitions across quarters (₹832 cr, ₹8,943 cr and ₹4,644 cr are not on the same basis), so I relied on NII, PAT and the bank KPIs rather than its auto-computed trajectory signals. For a lender, the right yardstick is price-to-book against return on equity. At 1.95× book, with ROE of 11.7% trailing and about 13.6% in the latest quarter, the stock is fairly valued, not cheap. That is a premium to peers: P71 on P/B (+33% vs the 1.5× median) and P79 on forward P/E. The price is also at 97% of its 52-week range, which leaves limited upside unless ROE keeps rising. The main risks to the thesis are on the funding side. NIM has slipped from 3.74% in Q4 FY26 to 3.32%, deposits are growing slower than loans (18.6% vs 21.7%), and the CASA ratio of about 32% sits below the sector's 35–38% band.

drivers: Q2FY27 management raised guidance: deposits to 11-12% (from 9-11%), advances to 13-14% (from 11-13%), with an expected 5-6 bps NIM lift from the repo hike
The headline 14.71% profit growth is flattered by Rs.1,386 cr of one-time NSE listing gains; excluding them, core operating growth is about 18% and treasury income is softer

technical.setup: Breakout above the upper Bollinger band on rising, accumulation-backed volume, but the stock is stretched (RSI 73, %B 1.11, about 8% above its 20-day average), the trend is only early-stage (ADX 21.9), and the 50-day average still sits below the 200-day; under the current momentum regime an extended breakout is not a buy, so the better entry is a pullback toward the 857-863 average cluster.

trader.reasoning: We keep the 24 shares. Fundamentals look fair, not cheap: underlying profit growth is only high single digits once the one-off NSE listing gain is removed, margins are slipping, credit costs are rising, and deposits are growing slower than loans. Sentiment is positive on the raised guidance and buying in the Financials sector, but results day got only a muted reaction. The analysts also disagree on how strong core profit growth is, so we give sentiment less weight. Technically the stock is stretched after a breakout (RSI 73, trading above the upper Bollinger band) with only an early-stage trend, and this momentum regime blocks adding to extended names; the better re-entry is a pullback toward the 857-863 support zone. We do not trim, because nothing in the thesis has broken, the position is small at 2.4% of the portfolio, and a sale now would likely be taxed as a short-term gain at 20% on the roughly 2,500 rupee profit. The stop sits just below the 863 support (ATR was not provided).

fundamental.thesis: Indian Bank is a mid-sized public-sector bank with a ₹8.74L cr deposit base and ₹7.11L cr of advances, and about two-thirds of its loans go to retail, agriculture and MSME borrowers (RAM 65%). In H1FY27 total income grew 16.1% YoY to ₹44,333 cr and PAT grew 28.1% to ₹6,897 cr, but Q2 includes a one-off NSE listing gain of ₹1,387 cr. Stripping it out, underlying PAT growth looks closer to high single digits, and the core trend is mixed. Gross NPA improved from 2.23% to 1.86% to 1.61% with PCR at 98%. Against that, NIM slipped from 3.37% to 3.24%, credit cost rose from 0.21% to 0.47% to 0.71% over three quarters, and deposits are growing slower than loans (12.5% vs 17.5% YoY). Using P/B against ROE (the lender yardstick), 1.44x book for a 15.4% ROE is cheap in absolute terms, but peers are similar: P/B is only at P43 and P/E (9.9x) at P29 among regional banks, so the grade is fair. Analysts raised FY EPS estimates by about 5% over 90 days, which supports the case. The main risk is that loans keep growing faster than deposits, pushing up funding costs and squeezing NIMs further just as credit costs rise.

drivers: Management kept FY27 ROA guidance unchanged at 1.0% (H1 tracking 0.9%) and expects Q3 margins flat with a slight negative bias. The Supreme Court's AT-1 write-down reversal cuts CET-1 by about 240 bps (13.7% to 11.4%), which is a material capital concern.
Market reaction to Q2 results was in line (-1.2% over 1 and 2 days) despite 65% YoY profit growth. Investors did not reward the headline beat, likely because of the AT-1 capital overhang.

On trailing P/E, the main yardstick for this asset-light business, valuation is fair at 26.0x, inside the 22-30x sector range and near the 26.9x peer median (P46), and the near-52-week-low price and EV/EBITDA discount (10.8x vs 15.2x) look less compelling because TTM EBITDA of about Rs 1,140 cr implies closer to 12.8x, while the 17.6x forward P/E requires about 48% EPS growth even as FY estimates were cut 10.5% in 30 days; the 23.62 debt/equity and 136% dividend yield appear to be data errors given Rs 507 cr of net cash, so neither was used. The biggest risk is that earnings keep falling as estimates are cut, with weak cash conversion (H1 CFO/PAT 0.50x, FCF Rs 6 cr), so the stock could be a falling knife rather than a value entry.

Alkem is a leading India branded-formulations maker (number 3 by prescriptions, 15 brands ranked in the top 3, about 68% of sales from India), with smaller US generics, biotech (Enzene) and a newly acquired MedTech arm (Occlutech). Q2FY27 revenue grew 13.8% YoY to ₹4,552 cr, with gross margin up 220 bps to 67.2% and EBITDA margin at 22.5%, but consolidated PAT fell 14.4% YoY to ₹667 cr (PAT margin 14.7%, down from 17.0% in Q3FY26) because of a higher tax rate. Underneath that, India sales grew only 9.5% against IPM growth of 13.8%, and US growth slowed sharply from +20.3% in FY26 to +2.4% on mid-teens price erosion. Using trailing P/E as the yardstick for a branded-formulations name, the stock trades at 27.4x, about 25% below the peer median of 36.4x (P31) and at the lower edge of the 28-40x sector band, while EV/EBITDA of 20.2x is near the peer median (P46); taken together this is fair to slightly cheap. The main risks are the Daman OAI status, continued Enzene losses, and EPS estimates cut 3.1% over 90 days.

fundamental.thesis: Ajanta Pharma is a branded-generics maker focused on chronic therapies: about 66% of revenue comes from branded generics across India (30%), Asia (18%) and Africa (18%), and US generics add 29%. In India it ranks #1 in ophthalmology and is the 4th fastest-growing of the top 25 companies, growing about 1.27x the Indian pharma market (16.7% vs 13.2%). Growth is speeding up. Revenue growth rose from +14% (Q2FY26) to +20% (Q3FY26) and +25% (Q1FY27), and reached about +32.5% in Q2FY27 (₹1,794 cr, implied from H1 ₹3,420 cr less Q1 ₹1,626 cr). Implied Q2 PAT of ₹388 cr is up about 49%, and PAT margin widened to about 21.6% from 19%, though cash conversion is only moderate (CFO/PAT 0.86x in H1). On the healthcare yardstick of trailing P/E plus peer rank, valuation is fair. Trailing P/E of 35.4x sits inside the 28-40x sector band and at P46 vs peers, and forward P/E of 26.3x signals expected earnings growth. EV/EBITDA of 24.3x (P69) and P/B of 8.3x (P77) carry a premium that a 25% ROE broadly justifies. The biggest risk is the 29% US generics exposure: generics are tariff-exempt for now, but the pending US Commerce review of generics plus forex losses already hitting reported profit could stall the margin gains, and management has given no forward guidance.

Bharat Forge is a global forging and components supplier for trucks, cars and industrial uses, with a fast-growing defence arm; it sits with the global-platform auto ancillaries, so it depends on EU and US truck cycles and tariffs more than on Indian auto demand. Consolidated revenue grew +19.8% YoY to ₹9,510 cr in H1 FY27, up from about +11% in FY26, helped by defence revenue rising about 47%; the implied Q2 FY27 is roughly ₹4,870 cr revenue and ₹279 cr PAT after a ₹-90 cr Q1 loss. Reported H1 PAT fell 67.7% to ₹189 cr because of restructuring charges at the German subsidiary BF CDP and the Tork Motors insolvency, and EBITDA margin slipped from 17.4% in FY26 to 15.3%. Valuation is expensive: I graded on EV/EBITDA because this is a capital-intensive business, and at 33.4× it is about 75% above the 19.1× auto-parts peer median (P80); trailing P/E of 86× and P/B of 9.7× are the highest among peers (P100), and ROE is only 11.6% with the stock at 88% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is that a defence-led growth story is priced in while sell-side EPS estimates are being cut (FY -11.3% over 90 days), H1 free cash flow was ₹-616 cr, and the European and US subsidiaries are still running at weak 3.5–4% EBITDA margins.

fundamental.thesis: MRF is India's largest tyre maker, with a net-cash balance sheet (about ₹1,850 cr net cash, AAA rating), and sells to both carmakers and the replacement market at home and abroad. Sales are growing well but profits are shrinking: H1 FY27 revenue rose 13.4% YoY to ₹17,076 cr while PAT fell 14.3% to ₹882 cr. Working out Q2 FY27 alone (H1 minus Q1), revenue rose about 17% to roughly ₹8,660 cr but PAT fell about 26% to roughly ₹387 cr, a margin of about 4.5%. PAT margin has slid from 8.5% (Q3 FY26) to 7.8%, 5.9% and 5.2%, and EBITDA margin is down 268 bps YoY to 12.2% as raw materials eat 72.7% of revenue. On valuation (P/E as the sector card prescribes for Auto, with EV/EBITDA as a cross-check), trailing P/E of 22.5x sits inside the 18–28x Auto band, so I grade it fair rather than cheap. The deep discount to the 'Auto Parts' peer median (39x P/E, 19x EV/EBITDA) mostly reflects a mismatched peer set and falling earnings, not mispricing; the forward P/E of 19.2x relies on estimates that were cut 8.3% over 90 days. The biggest risk is that margins keep compressing: free cash flow turned negative (₹-371 cr in H1, cash flow from operations only 0.72x PAT) and inventory jumped 32% to ₹7,163 cr, which could mean demand is softening or the company is building stock ahead of further price or cost pressure.

fundamental.thesis: Tube Investments of India is a high-ROIC diversified engineering conglomerate (core segment ROCE 44–49%) spanning precision tubes, metal-formed products, industrial chains, a 56.3% stake in CG Power (power equipment), and a nascent EV mobility business — positioning it across India's capital-goods and energy-transition cycles. Q1FY27 consolidated revenue grew +17.1% YoY to ₹6,215 cr (consistent with FY26's +17.5%), but PAT declined -3.0% YoY to ₹294 cr as PAT margin compressed to 4.73% from 5.71% YoY — EBITDA margin has contracted sequentially from 12.6% (9M FY26) to 11.6% (FY26) to 10.6% (Q1FY27), driven primarily by the EV segment's ₹147 cr PBT loss in the quarter. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive conglomerate (27.4× vs sector peer median 34.0×, P29 percentile), the stock grades fair; trailing P/E of 84.75× sits at P88 vs peers and well above the Industrials ceiling of 45×, but this is inflated by EV-loss-suppressed current earnings, and forward P/E of 35.05× (near sector median) implies the market is already pricing in meaningful earnings recovery — leaving limited valuation buffer if that recovery is delayed. The biggest near-term risk is the EV segment burning roughly ₹147 cr in PBT per quarter with no stated path to breakeven, while sell-side EPS estimates have been cut -12% over both 30 and 90 days — a warning that consensus may need further downward adjustment before a re-rating.

Cummins India is the market leader in diesel and gas engines and gensets in India, and data-centre backup power has risen to about 40% of its power-generation mix (from 23% a year ago), with a clean balance sheet holding about ₹2,196 cr of net cash. H1 FY27 revenue grew 10.7% YoY to ₹6,727 cr, but PAT fell 8.9% to ₹1,116 cr and PAT margin compressed from 19.4% to 15.9%; with Q1 at +18%, the implied Q2 revenue growth is only about +4%, so growth has sharply decelerated while EBITDA fell 11.4%. In Q2FY27 consolidated income rose 18.8% YoY to Rs 11,388 cr and PAT rose 25.2% to Rs 1,520 cr (13.3% margin), driven by CIFCL (disbursements +47%, PAT +41% to Rs 1,630 cr). Using P/B against sustainable ROE, the right yardstick for a lender holdco, the stock trades at 1.86x book with an implied ROE of about 17% (trailing P/E 10.8x, forward 8.0x). The biggest risk is that the parent's earnings depend on a single lender's credit cycle while the insurance subsidiary drags on profits, and FY earnings estimates have already been cut 6.1% over 90 days.

fundamental.thesis: Indian Energy Exchange runs India's dominant power exchange, an asset-light trading platform where most revenue (77-78%) comes from transaction fees. Real-Time Market volumes have grown from 20% of its electricity volumes in FY23 to 41% in H1 FY27. In Q2FY27 revenue rose +10.8% YoY to ₹203 cr and PAT rose +12.9% to ₹139 cr, a 68.5% PAT margin. Revenue growth has slowed from +19.3% in Q1FY26 and +14.6% for FY26 to roughly 10-11% over the last three periods, though margins are steady to rising. Cash conversion is only moderate, with CFO/PAT of 0.73x in H1FY27 versus 0.88x in FY26. Because this is a fee-based exchange rather than a lender, I graded it on P/E and EV/EBITDA, not the bank P/B yardstick. On that basis it looks cheap: trailing P/E of 22.3x is 37% below the broad-market median of 35.2x, EV/EBITDA of 14.2x is at P24, ROE is 39%, and the stock sits at about 9% of its 52-week range. Part of that discount is fair given the regulatory overhang, and next-year earnings estimates have been cut 5.5% over 90 days, so the stock is not mispriced beyond doubt.

IFCI is a government-controlled development finance institution with a legacy stressed loan book, and most of its consolidated revenue comes from subsidiaries rather than new lending. The H1 FY27 results filed on 2026-11-12 were not extracted, so the latest usable full-year figures are FY26: revenue of 2,069 cr (+2.5% YoY) and PAT of 181 cr (+5.7%), with an 8.7% PAT margin. Growth has slowed from +13.4% in H1 FY26 to +2.5% for the full year, and the loan book shrank 23.6% YoY. Asset quality is very poor: gross NPA is about 96–99%, and the H1 FY27 KPIs show net NPA rising to 95.6% and capital adequacy (CRAR) at a negative 18.4%. Using the lender yardstick of price-to-book versus sustainable ROE, a P/B of 2.43x is expensive for a business with ROA of about 0.7%, a negative capital ratio and an impaired book. The 119x trailing P/E (P96 vs the broad market) points the same way, and the lower 23x forward P/E is not credible without a visible lending turnaround. The biggest risk is that the stock's run to 73% of its 52-week range rests on government-ownership and re-rating hopes rather than earnings power. Any further deterioration in book value or capital could force dilution or restructuring.

fundamental.thesis: Redington is one of India's largest IT and mobility distributors, with operations across India, the Middle East, Africa and Turkey. It is tagged Industrials here, but it is really a thin-margin, working-capital-heavy distribution business, so the order-book sector card does not apply. On the latest officially extracted quarter, Q1 FY27, revenue grew 34.6% YoY to ₹34,922 cr and PAT rose 94.6% to ₹453 cr. Revenue growth has re-accelerated from +15.7% in Q3 FY26 and +22.1% in Q1 FY26. PAT margin is stable-to-improving but razor-thin, at 1.3% versus 1.1–1.4% across the window. The Q2 FY27 results are filed but not yet extracted; the unverified yfinance figure of ₹41,405 cr revenue and ₹541 cr PAT suggests the momentum continued. Valuation uses EV/EBITDA and P/E against the broad market, because there are no tight distribution peers and the IT-services P/E band does not fit. At 9.4x EV/EBITDA and 14.3x trailing / 10.1x forward P/E, it sits at P9–P13 of the broad market, which is cheap. Sell-side EPS estimates were raised 6.7% over 30 days. The biggest risk is cash conversion: FY26 CFO/PAT was only 0.16x, so profits are being absorbed by receivables and inventory.

fundamental.thesis: R R Kabel is a mid-sized wires and cables maker with a smaller, loss-making FMEG (fans, lights, appliances) arm. Wires and cables bring in about 91% of H1 revenue (₹5,890 cr, up 54.8%), so the company rides the same power, real-estate and data-centre demand as the bigger cable makers. Growth is strong: H1 FY27 revenue rose 52.8% to ₹6,452 cr and PAT rose 87.2% to ₹386 cr. Taking H1 minus Q1 gives Q2 FY27 revenue of about ₹3,284 cr (+51.8% YoY) and PAT of about ₹181 cr (+56%). That is still faster than the +19.5% of a year ago, but the Q2 PAT margin slipped to about 5.5% from 6.5% in Q1, and EBITDA margin fell from 10.4% to roughly 9.2%. So profitability is rising year on year but has come off its Q1 peak. On EV/EBITDA, the yardstick this sector card calls for, the stock trades at 32.0×, about 37% above the broad-market median (P67). Trailing P/E is 52.7× (P71) against a forward P/E of 34.0×. That multiple sits above the static 28–45× industrials P/E band, but the forward P/E and roughly 21% ROE give a fair, fully priced grade rather than a cheap one, especially with the stock at 94% of its 52-week range. There are no tight cable peers in the comparison set, so the peer rank is only broad-market context. The biggest weakness is cash: H1 operating cash flow was only 0.31× PAT and free cash flow was -₹159 cr. Capex of ₹280 cr in H1 pushed net debt from ₹147 cr to ₹455 cr and finance costs rose 87%. Real leverage is still modest at roughly 0.18× equity; the 13.09 debt/equity figure in the snapshot is most likely a percentage, not a multiple.

fundamental.thesis: RVNL is a state-owned rail and infrastructure EPC contractor that earns its revenue by executing an order book, much of it from the Ministry of Railways, with newer wins in power (DVC MoU) and overseas (MEA award); no order-book cover or inflow figure was provided, so revenue visibility could not be graded. In Q1 FY27, revenue grew +10.6% YoY to Rs 4,321 cr and PAT grew +18.7% to Rs 160 cr, an improvement on the -4.0% revenue and -39.9% PAT decline in Q1 FY26 and on the weak FY26 (revenue +2.5%, PAT -31.5%); however, PAT margin is still a thin 3.7%, and the trend table mixes cumulative periods (H1/9M/FY), so the acceleration rests on one quarter. Using EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for order-book and capital-intensive businesses, the stock is expensive at 70.3x (P95 vs the broad market, +201% vs median), with a trailing P/E of 59.0x above the 28-45x Industrials range and P/B of 5.2x against a 9% ROE, even though the price is near its 52-week low (14% of range). The biggest risks are the Q2 FY27 results due 12 Nov 2026, which will test management's guidance of ~15% revenue and 15-20% PAT growth while sell-side FY EPS estimates have been cut 12.5-20%, and the Rs 890 cr KRCL interest dispute, which equals more than a full year of PAT.

Schneider Electric Infrastructure makes electrical distribution and grid-automation equipment such as switchgear, transformers and substation automation, and it sits in the power-transmission and data-centre capex theme that the sector card rates as the richest-priced part of Industrials. In Q2FY27, revenue grew +19.8% YoY to Rs 779 cr, picking up from +4.8% in Q1FY27, but PAT fell -43.3% YoY to Rs 29.65 cr. PAT margin compressed from 8.0% to 3.8% YoY and EBITDA margin from 13.6% to 8.4%, after Q1FY27 PAT had already fallen -69.8%. H1 operating cash flow also turned negative (Rs -29 cr vs +Rs 84 cr a year ago) as inventory built up, so profits are not converting to cash. Using EV/EBITDA as the yardstick for a capital-goods name, 76.6x (P96 vs the broad market, median 23.3x) is at the top of even the 50-80x electricals band, and trailing P/E of 146.8x is far above the 28-45x Industrials range, so the stock is expensive. The biggest risk is that the market is pricing a margin recovery that has not yet appeared: sell-side FY EPS estimates have been cut 30% in 30 days and 44% in 90 days while the stock trades near its 52-week high, and no order-book or inflow data was available to show demand visibility.

fundamental.thesis: Shipping Corporation of India is India's largest state-owned shipping company, running tankers, liner, bulk carriers and offshore vessels. It is a freight-rate-driven, capital-intensive cyclical, so the Industrials order-book sector card does not really apply. H1 FY27 revenue rose 55.8% YoY to ₹4,137 cr and PAT rose 120.4% to ₹1,197 cr, faster than Q1 FY27 (+40.3% revenue, +74.9% PAT) and FY26 (+3.1% revenue). PAT margin widened to 28.9% from 20.5% a year ago, cash backed the profit (CFO/PAT 1.10x), and tankers led the growth (+62.5%, 44% PBIT margin), helped by Middle East disruption. On the yardsticks for a capital-intensive lender-funded shipper, EV/EBITDA and P/B, the stock looks cheap: P/B is 1.69x and trailing P/E is 10.65x against a broad-market median of about 35x. The live EV/EBITDA (35x), forward P/E (94x), dividend yield (424%) and debt/equity (29.45) readings look broken and were not used. My rough check puts EV/EBITDA near 5x on trailing EBITDA of about ₹3,500 cr. But these are probably peak-cycle, geopolitics-boosted earnings, and the stock is already at 66% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is that tanker rates fall back as Middle East disruption eases. On top of that come stress in the LNG joint ventures (₹240 cr ILT-3 provision; auditors flag going-concern doubts at ILT-1/2/3), board committees still short of SEBI listing-rule requirements, and a government stake sale stuck since 2020.

Techno Electric is a mid-sized power transmission and distribution EPC contractor that is exposed to India's grid-capex upcycle, and it holds a large net cash pile of about ₹2,031 cr. In H1 FY27, revenue grew 26.9% YoY to ₹1,738 cr and PAT rose 4.9% to ₹252 cr (17.1% on continuing operations), a 14.5% PAT margin. Growth has slowed from +43% in FY26 to +20-27% now, and EBITDA margin has slipped from 20-21% to 19.3%; the order-book and order-inflow figures needed to judge future revenue are missing from the data. Using EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick for this capital-heavy business, 19.4x sits near the peer middle (P40, 17% below median), and the 26.2x trailing P/E is just under the 28-45x Industrials range. I grade it fair rather than cheap because FY EPS estimates were cut 14.9% in 30 days and cash conversion is weak, with CFO/PAT at 0.19x in H1 and negative in FY26. The biggest risk is that profits are not turning into cash: ₹590 cr of Afghanistan receivables depend on an uncertain ADB/UNOPS payment process, and a ₹212 cr arbitration has been pending since 2012.

fundamental.thesis: Tega Industries makes wear-resistant consumables and equipment for mining and mineral processing, and its June 2026 acquisition of Molycop has made it a much larger, globally leveraged business. In the last extracted quarter (Q1 FY27), consolidated revenue jumped to about ₹1,720 cr from about ₹372 cr a year earlier, but this came mainly from adding one month of Molycop. Organically, the legacy Tega business grew revenue 21% and consumables grew 36% with a 24.1% margin, while equipment revenue fell 44%. Before the deal, growth was already slowing: FY26 revenue rose only 3.2% and PAT fell 28.9%, and Q3 FY26 revenue declined 1.4% with PAT down 63.7%. On the yardstick the sector card prescribes for this business (EV/EBITDA), the stock is expensive at 51.7x, above the 90th percentile of the broad market, and its trailing P/E of 88.8x is well above the 28-45x Industrials range. The 48.4x forward P/E implies a recovery that sell-side estimates are cutting sharply (FY EPS down 51% in 30 days). The biggest risk is the heavy debt taken on for Molycop: deleveraging depends on integration and working capital going to plan, while Q2 FY27 results filed on 2026-11-08 are not yet reflected in this data.

fundamental.thesis: Titagarh Rail Systems is a mid-sized Indian rail equipment maker (freight wagons, metro and passenger coaches) that depends on Indian Railways and metro capex orders. Revenue has slowed rather than accelerated: deriving Q2 FY27 from the filings (H1 FY27 ₹1,558 cr minus Q1 ₹765 cr) gives about ₹793 cr, only +0.6% YoY against ₹788 cr, down from +12.6% in Q1. Q2 PAT of about ₹63 cr (7.9% margin, versus 6.0% a year ago) and an H1 EBITDA margin of 13.8% (from 11.1%) show better profitability. However, the +375% H1 PAT jump is flattered by restated prior-year Firema losses, and H1 free cash flow was negative at about ₹-77 cr after ₹230 cr of capex. On valuation, I used EV/EBITDA, as the sector card recommends for order-book businesses: 35.8x is in the top quartile of the market (P75, +54% above the median), and trailing P/E of 103x is far above the 28–45x Industrials range. That is rich for a business earning a 4.9% ROE with a P/B of 5.2x, sitting at about 90% of its 52-week high, so I grade it expensive. The forward P/E of 26.4x only looks reasonable if the sell-side's recovery happens, yet FY EPS estimates have been cut 9% over 90 days while all 9 analysts still rate it a buy. That is a classic pre-derating pattern, and the order-book and order-inflow data needed to check revenue visibility is missing from the pack.

fundamental.thesis: Tata Motors (TMCV) is India's largest commercial vehicle maker, with 36.2% domestic share in H1 FY27 and 55.7% in heavy trucks, and it holds net cash of Rs 15,900 cr before the Iveco deal. Revenue growth accelerated from +16.1% in Q3 FY26 to +19.3% in Q1 FY27 and +36.3% in Q2 FY27 (Rs 25,338 cr on 42% wholesale volume growth), but EBITDA margin slipped from 11.3% to 10.9% YoY and PAT fell from Rs 2,556 cr in Q1 to Rs 1,253 cr in Q2 (5.0% margin) after a Rs 708 cr fair-value loss; management guides to tapering growth and a 150-200 bps commodity headwind in Q3, so the pre-computed 'expanding' PAT margin signal and the 17.1% Q1 EBITDA margin (it conflicts with 10.9% for both H1 and Q2) should not be relied on. Valuation is fair using EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for this capital-intensive business: 16.8x is 28% below the broad-market median of 23.3x (P30), and forward P/E of 18.5x sits at the low end of the 18-28x auto range with estimates up 10.1% over 90 days, but the trailing P/E of 49.5x (distorted by fair-value losses) and P/B of 11.8x (P87) limit the cheapness case, and the peer set is a broad-market fallback rather than true CV peers. The biggest risk is the Iveco acquisition, whose final tender outcome, funding and integration burden are not visible in the data provided and could erode the net cash position just as the CV cycle's growth rates are guided to slow, while the auditor resignation filed on 2026-10-31 remains unexplained here.

Triveni Turbine is a midcap maker of industrial steam turbines (mainly up to 100 MW) and aftermarket services, selling to process industries and power producers in India and abroad, with a net-cash balance sheet of about ₹165 crore. H1 FY27 revenue rose only 6.4% YoY to ₹934 crore, while PAT fell 33% to ₹104 crore; EBITDA margin dropped from 26.0% to 17.7% and PAT margin from about 16% to 11.2%, so revenue growth is slowing (+19.2% in Q1 to +6.4% for H1) while profitability shrinks. On EV/EBITDA, the yardstick the Industrials card names for order-book businesses, the stock trades at 45.5x (P86 vs the broad market). Trailing P/E is 61.3x, above the 28–45x Industrials range, and P/B is 14.8x (P93), so I grade it expensive. The main risk is the de-rating the sector card warns about: consensus FY EPS has been cut 12.2% over 90 days while 6 of 9 analysts still rate it a buy, and no order-book or order-inflow data was provided to show the margin squeeze is temporary.

Revenue growth picked up from about +1-3% through FY26 to +12.4% in Q1 FY27, but slowed again in Q2 FY27: Q2 revenue is about ₹1,113 cr, up roughly 6.2% YoY (worked out as H1 ₹2,281 cr minus Q1 ₹1,168 cr). Profit is moving the wrong way. Q2 PAT is about ₹249 cr, down roughly 10% YoY, H1 PAT fell 5.5% to ₹550 cr, and EBITDA margin has dropped from 39.9% to 34.5% at the H1 level (about 32% in Q2 alone) over six periods. On the positive side, H1 cash conversion recovered to 1.18x CFO/PAT. Because the business is capital-intensive I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA: at 27.4x it is about 18% above the broad-market median, while trailing P/E of 30.7x sits inside the 28-45x Industrials band, so valuation is fair rather than cheap, especially with margins still falling. The biggest worry is that sell-side EPS estimates have been cut 8.6% in 30 days while 9 of 13 analysts still rate it a buy, a pattern that often comes before a de-rating.

fundamental.thesis: Apar Industries is a leading Indian maker of power-transmission conductors, specialty oils and cables, and it benefits directly from the grid-capex cycle. H1 FY27 revenue rose +25.0% YoY to ₹13,522 cr, and Q2 alone grew +21.3% to ₹6,931 cr. Revenue growth has held steady at +22% to +25% over the trend window. PAT jumped +77.7% to ₹915 cr, PAT margin widened from 4.8% to 6.8% and EBITDA margin from 9.2% to 11.8%. The conductor order book is a record ₹12,025 cr (+67% YoY) and Q2 order inflow rose +123%. Volume quality is weaker than the headline, though: conductor volumes fell 8% and oil volumes fell 17% in H1. So growth is coming mainly from higher prices (elevated metal and base-oil costs passed on) and a richer product mix, not more units sold. Valuation is expensive. Graded on EV/EBITDA, the sector card's yardstick for capital-intensive names, it trades at 32.2x vs a peer median of 23.3x (P68). Trailing P/E is 59.2x, above the 28-45x Industrials band, at P77 on P/E and P90 on P/B. The stock sits at 90% of its 52-week range. The forward P/E of 46x and +21% upward revisions to FY EPS estimates offset this only partly. The biggest risk is earnings quality: H1 operating cash flow was -₹863 cr (CFO/PAT -0.94x) because of a ₹900+ cr inventory build and higher receivables, while US and export revenue are shrinking.

fundamental.thesis: BEML is a Schedule-'A' defence PSU under India's Ministry of Defence, manufacturing heavy equipment across mining, construction, defence platforms, and metro/rail segments, with revenue heavily dependent on government order execution. Q1FY27 revenue accelerated to ₹820 cr (+29.3% YoY from ₹634 cr) and the operating loss narrowed substantially (EBITDA swung from -₹41 cr to +₹3.6 cr YoY), yet PAT remained negative at -₹27 cr (-3.3% margin); more critically, FY26 full-year PAT collapsed 49.7% and order inflows landed at only ₹1,286 cr vs a ₹6,800 cr target — an 81% miss that is the single most important leading indicator for an order-book business. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for a capital-intensive industrial (Sector Card guidance), the stock trades at 48.4× (P88 among peers, 107% premium to sector median 23.3×) and trailing P/E of 94× versus the sector benchmark range of 28–45×, placing it firmly in expensive territory despite a more palatable forward P/E of 28× that already discounts a sharp earnings recovery. The biggest risk is that FY27 order inflows remain structurally below target, eroding book-to-revenue cover and triggering a 30–50% de-rating (consistent with Industrials sector card cycle-risk warning) before the earnings recovery the valuation demands actually materialises.

fundamental.thesis: Blue Dart Express is India's dominant integrated express logistics company and a DHL Group subsidiary, operating time-definite air and ground freight networks with significant pricing power in the premium segment. Q1FY27 showed a sharp positive inflection: revenue grew +15.0% YoY to ₹1,658 crore (accelerating from a flat +7% range across all FY26 quarters), while PAT surged 81.2% YoY to ₹88 crore with EBITDA margin expanding to 16.7% — the operating-leverage story is finally showing up in PAT. Using EV/EBITDA as the preferred yardstick for capital-intensive logistics (EV/EBITDA is unavailable in the snapshot), the fallback trailing P/E of 40.4× sits within the Industrials sector range of 28–45× (fair), but forward P/E at 26.5× — below the 28× lower bound — implies the market is pricing in substantial earnings growth; the stock at 10.6% of its 52-week range (near ₹4,883 vs a 52-week high of ₹7,036) at a fair-to-cheap forward multiple presents a potentially asymmetric setup, though the falling-knife risk at this proximity to the low demands caution. The single biggest fundamental risk is that crude oil at $89.72 and rising directly compresses unit economics since freight and handling costs constitute 58% of revenues, and the 90-day EPS revision of -24.3% signals the sell side is already cutting numbers — a classic pre-derating pattern that could undermine the inflection narrative.

fundamental.thesis: Carborundum Universal is a mid-cap maker of abrasives, industrial ceramics and electrominerals, with a large standalone India business and overseas subsidiaries in Russia, Germany and South Africa. Revenue growth has picked up from about +2-4% YoY through FY26 to +17.0% in Q1FY27 and +13.1% in Q2FY27 (₹1,455 cr), and standalone revenue grew 28% on Ceramics (+36%). Reported Q2 PAT, however, fell 83% to ₹12 cr (0.9% margin) because of an ₹80 cr charge for closing the German subsidiary CAAG. Before exceptional items, profit (PBEBT) rose 22% to ₹138 cr, but Abrasives grew only 4% and Electrominerals profit fell 21%. On EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for this capital-intensive Industrials name, the stock trades at 34.5x (P72 vs the broad market), and forward P/E is 40x (P82). The headline 115x P/E is inflated by the one-off charge. Against a 4.4% ROE and P/B of 5.8x, and with the price at 86% of its 52-week range, valuation looks expensive. Sell-side (4 sell, 2 hold) puts its mean target at roughly today's price. The biggest risk is the international subsidiaries: VAW in Russia is now on the US OFAC sanctions list, FZL in South Africa is being accounted for as not a going concern, and CAAG is winding down. Together they could bring more write-downs and keep weighing on reported earnings.

Cemindia Projects (formerly ITD Cementation, now Adani-promoted) is a mid-sized EPC contractor in marine, foundation, tunnelling and urban infrastructure work, with a record order book of ₹32,715 cr at Sept 30, 2026, up about 58% from ₹20,646 cr a year earlier and roughly 3.0x trailing-twelve-month revenue of about ₹10,800 cr. Execution has sped up: Q2 FY27 revenue rose 25.2% YoY to ₹2,749 cr, after +5.6% in Q1, and H1 revenue grew 14.6% to ₹5,470 cr. Profit quality is weaker than the topline: Q2 PAT rose 21.3% to ₹131 cr, but EBITDA margin slipped from 11.1% to 10.2% YoY, PAT margin is down to about 4.8%, and H1 operating cash flow was negative (CFO/PAT -0.29x) as contract assets rose by ₹474 cr. fundamental.thesis: Cochin Shipyard (COCHINSHIP) is India's largest PSU shipyard executing defence (Navy/Coast Guard) and commercial vessel contracts, backed by an order book of ₹21,100 cr (~5× annualised revenue) that provides multi-year execution visibility — structurally the most compelling asset on the balance sheet. Revenue growth has decelerated from +38.5% YoY in Q1 FY26 to +15.5% for 9M FY26, but more critically, PAT has swung sharply negative (-18.5% YoY in 9M FY26 vs +7.8% in Q1 FY26) as EBITDA margins compressed from 28.0% to 21.3% — a classic fixed-price-contract cost-creep pattern, likely driven by ISRF ramp-up overheads and higher input/subcontracting costs; cash conversion is deeply negative (CFO/PAT -2.40×, FCF -₹812 cr in H1 FY26), which is the most immediate red flag. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive model per the sector card, 45.51× sits at the upper bound of the 28–45× Industrials range and at P86 in the broad market (95% premium to median), grading expensive; the forward P/E discount (33.25× vs 54× trailing) signals the street is pricing in a sharp earnings recovery — but that recovery has not yet appeared in filed numbers and Q1 FY27 extraction is blank despite the August 2026 filing date. The single biggest risk is that margin compression deepens further on the ISRF ramp and rising crude-linked operating costs, in a RISK_OFF macro with D/E at 28.47 — any slippage in earnings recovery would unwind the current rich valuation quickly.
