fundamental.thesis: Indian Oil is India's largest state-run refiner and fuel marketer, so its earnings depend on government fuel-pricing policy as much as on crude prices: falling crude helps it, rising crude hurts. H1FY27 revenue rose 28.4% YoY to ₹549,972 cr and PAT rose 35.2% to ₹21,362 cr, but the half was very uneven: Q1 was a loss (₹-1,141 cr; EBITDA margin 1.9%), then Q2 PAT jumped to about ₹21,630 cr as refining margin (GRM) rose from $15.59 to $18.52/bbl. Revenue growth looks driven mostly by price rather than volume, since marketing sales fell from 26.2 to 25.2 MMT quarter-on-quarter and diesel sales from 10.9 to 9.0 MMT. On the yardstick the sector card names for oil marketing companies (P/E plus dividend yield, EV/EBITDA as a cross-check), the stock looks low on trailing numbers: P/E 4.4x against a peer median of 9.2x, EV/EBITDA 4.1x against 6.1x, and P/B 0.85x with 21% ROE. Those trailing numbers are inflated by an unusually strong Q2, though. Forward P/E is 7.7x, close to the 8.1x peer median and higher than trailing, which means analysts expect earnings to fall, so I grade it fair: priced for policy risk rather than mispriced. The biggest risk is crude at about $91 and rising while retail fuel prices stay frozen, which could push marketing margins back toward Q1-style losses; earnings are also turning into cash poorly (H1 CFO/PAT 0.48x, free cash flow ₹-1,450 cr).

Authum Investment & Infrastructure is a midcap NBFC and investment holding company. A large part of its earnings comes from investment and treasury income and from distressed-asset acquisitions; the latest is an NCLT-approved resolution plan announced on 2026-10-28. Its earnings are not steady lending income. In Q2FY27, revenue rose 12.6% YoY to ₹685 cr, but PAT fell 45.5% YoY to ₹418 cr. PAT margin dropped to 61.0%, from 74.6% in Q1FY27 and 71.0% for H1FY27. Revenue growth slowed from +21.4% in Q1 to +12.6% in Q2, and H1 PAT is down 10.6%. Cash backing for profits is weak: H1FY27 operating cash flow was -0.49x PAT and free cash flow was -₹763 cr. I graded valuation on P/B against ROE, the yardstick for lenders, not P/E. P/B of 2.91x with ROE of 13.1% is roughly fair, since the stock is neither under 1.5x nor above 3x with sub-12% ROE. The headline P/E of 8.95x sits at P5 of the broad market, but it is flattered by lumpy investment gains and should not be read as cheap. The main risk is that profits depend on market-linked and one-off gains that are not turning into cash. Thin lender disclosures (no NIM or GNPA data) and the reported 24.6 debt/equity also need checking against the filings.

Revenue is growing fast and the pace is picking up: up 22.8% YoY to ₹16,316 cr in H1FY27, against +0.5% in FY26 and -2.4% in 9M FY26. Implied Q2 revenue is about ₹8,055 cr (+26% YoY). Profit is not keeping pace, though. H1 PAT rose only 10.3% to ₹3,886 cr, the PAT margin slipped from 26.5% to 23.8%, and NIM eased from 1.55% to 1.48%, so earnings are rising more slowly than the loan book. I graded valuation on P/B against ROE, which is the right yardstick for a lender, not P/E. At 2.3x book for a 12.8–13.3% ROE and roughly 1.4% ROA, the stock is fair, maybe slightly full, for a low-margin, policy-driven financier. The 'cheap' peer reading (trailing P/E 18.7x, P20) compares IRFC with the whole market rather than with lenders, so I don't rely on it. The biggest risk is that further government stake sales add share supply while thin, shrinking spreads keep EPS growth near 10% even with strong loan growth.

fundamental.thesis: NIACL is India's largest PSU general insurer (85.44% government-owned), writing motor, health, marine, and fire coverage domestically and internationally, with a regulatory solvency ratio of 1.80×; however, the franchise is structurally loss-making at the underwriting level and profits depend entirely on investment income. Q1 FY27 delivered a net loss of ₹244 cr (vs. +₹392 cr in Q1 FY26, –162% YoY) as the incurred claim ratio worsened to 102.97% and the combined ratio deteriorated to 121.14%, confirming that claims and expenses together exceed earned premiums — both motor (–₹126 cr underwriting loss) and health (–₹134 cr) dragged, and net earned premium growth decelerated to just +1.9% YoY. Using P/B + ROE as the correct yardstick for an insurer (not P/E), P/B of 0.76× ranks NIACL at P1 in the broad peer set and appears cheap on its face, but a TTM ROE of only 3.4% fully explains this discount — it is structural cheapness, not mispricing — and analyst EPS estimates have been cut –47% in just 30 days, a classic pre-derating signal that the forward P/E of 9.2× bakes in recovery assumptions the combined-ratio trend does not yet support. The dominant near-term risk is a qualified audit conclusion on unreconciled reinsurance recoverable balances (₹75,490L gross, ₹13,783L doubtful-debt provision), compounded by a new CMD appointment in September 2026 and a mandatory Ind AS accounting transition due April 2027, leaving both governance and accounting transparency materially unresolved.

fundamental.thesis: Siemens Energy India (ENRIN) is a newly-listed (June 2025) power equipment company demerged from Siemens Limited, serving India's electrification build-out across power transmission (55.8% of revenue) and power generation (44.2%) — a structurally well-positioned business but with less than 18 months of standalone track record. Official 9M FY26 filings show revenue of ₹6,791 cr (+31.1% YoY) and PAT of ₹1,128 cr (+52.2%, 16.6% margin) with operating margins expanding 260 bps — a genuinely strong growth print — but three signals undercut the quality: (a) book-to-revenue declining from 2.25× (Q1) to 1.18× (H1), indicating execution outpacing new order wins; (b) Q2 CFO/PAT of just 0.09×, signalling earnings are not converting to cash; and (c) Power Transmission order backlog flat/down (-3.2% YoY) despite the headline growth. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive business (per sector card), ENRIN trades at 70.7× vs an Industrials benchmark of 28–45× implied equivalent — at P95 vs 473 listed peers on EV/EBITDA and P93 on trailing P/E of 102.8× — placing it unambiguously expensive at 90% of its 52-week range with zero valuation cushion. The stock is priced for prolonged flawless execution at peak cycle, and high financial leverage (D/E 4.48×) leaves no balance-sheet buffer if order inflows slow or margins disappoint.

The biggest risk is that revenue growth comes with falling margins and poor cash conversion while the stock is priced like a growth franchise. Separately, the ₹912 cr Q1 revenue from yfinance does not reconcile with the H1 total, and the 12% dividend yield in the snapshot is almost certainly a data error, so both should be checked.

fundamental.thesis: Sarda Energy and Minerals is a midcap integrated steel, ferro-alloys and power producer, with power as the largest profit driver (H1 FY27 revenue of Rs 1,739 cr at a 51% segment margin). Revenue growth has slowed sharply, from +51.6% in H1 FY26 to -3.2% in H1 FY27 (Rs 3,061 cr), partly against a high base; subtracting Q1 from H1 implies Q2 FY27 revenue of about Rs 1,453 cr (-4.9% YoY) and PAT of about Rs 287 cr (-11% YoY), though the H1 EBITDA margin rose to 43.3% from 40.4% and PAT was about flat (+0.8%). Using EV/EBITDA as the yardstick, I grade valuation as fair: 10.5x is above the 5-8x mid-cycle norm for steel cyclicals, which the high-margin power business partly justifies, while the 16.6x trailing P/E sits inside the 12-22x sector range; the 'cheap' peer verdict compares against the broad market rather than close peers, and the 11.0x forward P/E implies about 50% earnings growth that recent results do not yet show. The biggest risk is that earnings stay flat or fall if power weakens further (implied Q2 power revenue about -13% YoY, partly seasonal hydro) while steel stays soft, although the balance sheet looks manageable with net debt of about 0.9x EBITDA, H1 operating cash flow of Rs 981 cr, and the snapshot's 35.2 debt/equity most likely meaning 0.35x rather than very high leverage.

Pfizer Ltd is the Indian listed arm of Pfizer Inc., selling branded medicines in India, so it has little exposure to the US patented-drug tariff. It has net cash of ₹3,167 cr, a 47% ROCE and no subsidiaries. Revenue growth has held steady rather than accelerated. H1FY27 revenue rose 10.8% YoY to ₹1,380 cr. Q2FY27 revenue, derived as H1 minus Q1, was about ₹727 cr, roughly +13% YoY, after +8.3% in Q1. Reported H1 PAT jumped 35.9% to ₹518 cr, but that includes a one-time ₹132 cr payment for discontinuing Minipress XL. Stripping it out, underlying PAT grew only about 10%, and EBITDA margin has been choppy in the 38–46% range. On a trailing P/E yardstick (the right one for a branded-formulations business, with EV/EBITDA as a cross-check), the stock trades at 28.7x, at the low end of the 28–40x pharma band. It is also below the broad-market median (P39) on P/E and EV/EBITDA of 19.4x, and sits near its 52-week low (9.5% of range), so I grade it fair with a reasonable entry point rather than cheap. The trailing P/E is flattered by the exceptional gain, so the underlying multiple is about 30x. The biggest risk is the earnings path: cash from operations fell 40% in H1 (CFO/PAT 0.69x), sell-side next-year EPS estimates have been cut 4.3% over 90 days, and the parent's portfolio rationalisation could keep shrinking the product basket.

fundamental.thesis: K.P.R. Mill is a vertically integrated textile and garment maker with a smaller sugar business; textiles brought in Rs 2,979 cr of H1 FY27 revenue at a 21.7% margin, and sugar Rs 856 cr at 13.2%. Revenue growth has improved from -2.9% in Q3 FY26 to +9.3% in Q1 FY27 and +14.0% to Rs 3,875 cr in H1 FY27, while H1 PAT rose 40.1% to Rs 604 cr and implied Q2 (H1 minus Q1, not a reported figure) shows revenue of about Rs 1,905 cr (+15%) and PAT of about Rs 345 cr (+58%, 18.1% margin), though the filing data conflict on Q1 growth and on the H1 FY26 EBITDA margin (18.4% vs 20.1%), so these Q2 figures are approximate. Using EV/EBITDA as the yardstick for this capital-intensive business, valuation is fair: the listed 27.8x (P61, against a 23.3x broad-market median) and 46.9x trailing P/E appear to rest on FY26 earnings, and on my trailing-12-month estimates they fall to about 23x and 39x, offset by a 7.1x P/B on 16.2% ROE, a price at 85% of the 52-week range and only 5.6% upside to the mean analyst target. The biggest risk is that the margin jump proves temporary, because sugar's 42% growth supplied roughly half of H1 revenue growth and management gave no guidance; balance-sheet risk looks low, as the Rs 1,229 cr net cash and 2.19x CFO/PAT suggest the 10.46 debt/equity flag is a percentage (about 0.10x), although H1 cash conversion also ran high last year (2.84x) before falling to 1.28x for full-year FY26.

Sun TV Network is the dominant South Indian broadcaster, with 8 channels in 7 languages, the Sun NXT streaming app and three SunRisers cricket franchises, which are now a meaningful earnings engine (₹730 cr H1 revenue against ₹404 cr costs). H1 FY27 revenue fell 7.4% YoY to ₹2,398 cr, while PAT rose 11.3% to ₹984 cr (36.3% margin). The implied Q2 is weaker: revenue of about ₹940 cr against ₹1,300 cr a year ago, and PAT roughly flat at about ₹365 cr. The core TV business looks soft, with Q2 ad revenue down 13.5% YoY to ₹253 cr and subscription revenue up only 2.3%, and the trajectory signals show decelerating revenue and choppy, contracting PAT margins. On EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for this cash-generative media and capital-intensive franchise model, the stock trades at 4.6x versus a broad-market median of 23.3x (P2), with trailing P/E at 12.2x (P10) near its 52-week low, which grades as cheap. The biggest risk is that the cheapness reflects a structural decline in linear-TV advertising, with earnings increasingly tied to lumpy, cricket-calendar revenue.

fundamental.thesis: Trident is a Punjab-based home-textile and yarn maker that also runs a paper and chemicals business. In H1FY27 yarn is about 56% of revenue, towels about 35% and paper about 17%. H1FY27 revenue was flat at ₹3,506 cr (+0.3% YoY), but consolidated PAT jumped 44.5% to ₹334 cr on wider margins (EBITDA margin 18.6%, PAT margin 9.5%), with yarn EBIT nearly tripling to ₹337 cr. The implied Q2 is weaker on the top line: revenue of about ₹1,719 cr fell roughly 4% YoY after Q1's +4.7%, so revenue growth is decelerating even as PAT margin rose to about 10%. The table's 'accelerating' signal is unreliable because the older FY26 rows (₹171–670 cr) are clearly on a different basis. Because this is a capital-intensive manufacturer, I graded it mainly on EV/EBITDA: 15.7x is at P28 versus the broad market and below its median of 23.3x, and P/E of 35x trailing and 26x forward sits near the median. However, P/B of 2.8x against an ROE of only 8% is not cheap, so overall it is fair. The biggest risk is that the profit surge rests on one segment (yarn) while towels deteriorate (revenue -11%, EBIT -47%), just as the company commits to a ₹4,650 cr expansion worth about a third of its market cap.

fundamental.thesis: Vishal Mega Mart is a value-format hypermarket chain for middle- and lower-income shoppers, mainly in Tier-2/3 India. It has 819 stores as of Q1 FY27, up from 742 a year earlier, and same-store sales growth has held steady at 10-11%. Growth is slowing: the latest filing shows revenue of ₹3,877 cr (+13.5% YoY) and PAT of ₹338 cr (+9.8%), down from +18.7% revenue growth in Q1 FY27 and +20.4% in FY26. EBITDA margin slipped from 14.75% to 14.23% YoY, and PAT growing slower than revenue points to cost pressure. Cash conversion is strong: CFO/PAT is 2.2x, FCF is ₹673 cr and net debt is a minimal ₹137 cr. On valuation I graded on EV/EBITDA and P/E against the sector card's 60-100x norm for premium consumer names. A trailing P/E of 65.9x (44.2x forward) and EV/EBITDA of 29.1x put it at the low end of that band, so fair. It is still not cheap for mid-teens growth: it sits at P81 on P/E in a broad-market peer set, because there are no tight retail peers in the universe. The biggest risk is that growth keeps slowing while the stock carries a premium multiple. Analysts are trimming EPS estimates (FY next -2% over 90 days) while 18 of 19 still rate it a buy, a pattern that often comes before a de-rating. The extracted H1 figures (₹3,877 cr) also look inconsistent with Q1 alone (₹3,727 cr), so treat the trajectory numbers with caution.

The valuation snapshot's trailing P/E of 2.83× is almost certainly corrupted by the June 2026 5:1 bonus split distorting yfinance EPS; using trend-table LTM PAT of ~₹498 cr against ₹29,000 cr market cap implies an estimated trailing P/E of ~58×, well above the 18–28× Auto sector median — graded expensive — and the forward P/E of 38.28× (itself above sector median) confirms earnings are expected to remain well below recent peaks. Revenue growth accelerated from +18% in Q1 to about +26% in Q2 (roughly Rs 22,202 cr, derived as H1 minus Q1), and H1 volume growth of 11% extends the improvement from 2-3% in Q2-Q3 FY26 and 7% in Q1 FY27, but Q2 PAT swung from +48% to about -2% YoY (Rs 239 cr vs Rs 245 cr), partly due to a Bangladesh minimum tax, while PAT margin fell from 1.8% to about 1.1%, so the 'expanding' margin signal in the trend table, which mixes half-year and quarterly periods, looks unreliable. Using EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick, the stock looks fair, leaning cheap, at 9.0x (P8) and 20.7x trailing P/E near its 52-week low, because the broad-market peer set and 40-65x FMCG norm are poor comparisons for a 3% EBITDA-margin business, and 2.29x book for an estimated 11% ROE is not a clear bargain; the 54% dividend yield and 10.62 debt/equity look like data errors (debt/equity is probably about 0.11x), and the +55.6% consensus upside looks overstated because the implied price is below the 52-week low. fundamental.thesis: Sagility is a mid-cap healthcare outsourcing company. About 90% of revenue comes from US health insurers (payers) and about 10% from hospitals and other providers. It is tagged IT here, but its demand comes from US healthcare operations, not tech spending. In Q2FY27 revenue was ₹2,032 cr, up 22.5% YoY, and PAT was ₹284 cr, up 13.3%. Growth has slowed from +35.7% (Q3FY26) to +29.1% (FY26) to +25.0% (H1) to +22.5%, and constant-currency growth is only about 12%, so roughly half the headline growth comes from the weak rupee. Reported PAT margin fell to 14.0% from 15.1% a year ago, and adjusted PAT grew only 8.1% even though adjusted EBITDA margin reached a six-quarter high of 26.3%. On valuation, using P/E and EV/EBITDA, the trailing P/E of 21.5x is below the IT sector's 22–30x range and sits at about the 24th percentile of the broad market (there are no close peers in the universe). EV/EBITDA is 11.4x, forward P/E is 15.4x, and cash conversion is strong (CFO/PAT 1.27x), so the stock looks cheap. The biggest risk is client concentration: the top 3 clients are 60% of revenue and the top 10 are 84%, and voluntary attrition is high at 25.7%. Losing or repricing a single large client could hurt badly. The yfinance dividend yield (44%) and debt/equity (11.5) figures look like unit errors, so I ignored them.

NLC India is a state-owned lignite miner and power generator. It earns mostly regulated returns on thermal capacity, and it is growing its renewables business, where generation rose 31.9% in H1FY27. Revenue growth is solid: H1FY27 revenue was Rs 9,449 cr (+18.1% YoY). Working back from H1 and Q1, Q2FY27 revenue was about Rs 4,732 cr (+13.3% YoY), slower than Q1's +23.2%. Profit is much less steady. Q1FY27 PAT fell 46% to Rs 429 cr (9.1% margin), while implied Q2 PAT was about Rs 1,335 cr (roughly +114% YoY, 28% margin), which may include one-off regulatory items. The EBITDA margin trend is down, from 37–38% to about 30.5% for FY26. On valuation I used EV/EBITDA and P/B plus ROE, as the sector card suggests for capital-intensive regulated utilities. EV/EBITDA is 9.9x, P/B is 2.1x against a 16% ROE, and trailing P/E is 12.75x, which sits inside the 10–18x utilities range. So I grade it fair, not cheap. It only looks deeply cheap against the broad market, which is not a fair comparison for a regulated power company. The main risk is heavy debt-funded capex: debt/equity is 0.82, FY26 free cash flow was -Rs 2,779 cr, and the government's newly announced offer-for-sale (OFS) adds supply pressure on the share price.

fundamental.thesis: Zen Technologies makes combat-training simulators and counter-drone systems, and is a niche midcap that benefits as India shifts defence buying to domestic suppliers (about 82% of recently approved capital proposals are earmarked for Indian industry). Revenue is very uneven from quarter to quarter: Q2FY27 revenue was a record ₹345 cr, up 98.8% YoY, right after Q1FY27 fell 10.5% to ₹142 cr. That took H1FY27 revenue to ₹487 cr (+46.7%), but H1 PAT grew only 15.7% to ₹124 cr. Margins are shrinking, with H1 EBITDA margin down from 39.0% to 35.1% and PAT margin down from 32.3% to 25.5%, partly because other income fell 24%. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the sector card's yardstick for order-book businesses, and the stock is expensive: EV/EBITDA is 68.3x (P94 vs peers, +193% vs the 23.3x median) and trailing P/E is 87x, well above the 28–45x Industrials range. The 32.9x forward P/E already assumes a sharp earnings recovery, and analysts raising estimates by about 4–5% only partly supports that. The biggest risk is that the ₹1,376 cr order book covers only about 1.6x trailing-12-month revenue (about ₹880 cr), and new orders arrive in lumps. That gives only around 1.5 years of visibility, so one slow quarter could hurt a stock priced for steady execution.

fundamental.thesis: Hindustan Zinc is India's dominant integrated zinc-lead-silver miner (Vedanta Group subsidiary) with near-monopoly status in domestic mined zinc and structural cost advantages that produce world-class EBITDA margins of 62.4% — a level no domestic peer can match. H1FY27 revenue surged 76.7% YoY to ₹28,840 cr (accelerating sharply from -4.4% in Q1FY26), PAT grew 143.4% YoY to ₹11,881 cr, and PAT margin expanded to 41.2% from 29.9% — a five-period trajectory of simultaneously accelerating revenue growth and expanding margins driven primarily by elevated zinc and silver commodity prices, with cash quality strong (CFO/PAT 1.12×). Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive commodity miner, the stock trades at 10.59× — P13 among 473 peers and a 54.6% discount to the broad-market EV/EBITDA median — with trailing P/E of 17.46× squarely inside the Materials sector range (12–22×), grading cheap on peer-relative metrics, though 10.59× sits above the 5–8× typical mid-cycle range for base-metals cyclicals, signalling that some commodity-cycle-peak risk remains unpriced. The thesis is materially constrained by an unresolved ED/FEMA investigation (search and seizure June 2026, no regulatory communication as of the October 2026 filing) and SEBI observations on related party transaction disclosures — governance headwinds typical of Vedanta Group that can trigger a de-rating independent of commodity fundamentals, and are weighted heavily under the midcap governance overlay.

Jubilant Ingrevia is a mid-cap Indian chemicals maker with three segments: Specialty Chemicals, Nutrition (vitamin B3 and feed premixes) and Chemical Intermediates (acetyls). It is now adding CDMO capacity and has bought a 40% stake in ZettaOne, an electronics-materials business. Q2FY27 revenue was ₹1,394 cr, up 24% YoY and an all-time high, compared with low-single-digit growth through FY26 (+1.3% in Q1FY26, +5.0% for FY26). PAT rose 61% to ₹111 cr, and both PAT margin (8.0% vs 6.1–7.2% across FY26) and EBITDA margin (16.0% vs 13.6–14.8%) widened, but Q1FY27 is missing from the filings data, so the speed-up rests mainly on one quarter. I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA, as the sector card says to for chemicals: at 18.1x it is far above the card's 5–8x mid-cycle range for commodity chemicals, though that range doesn't fully fit a specialty/CDMO mix; it is 22% below the broad-market median (P35), with trailing P/E of 34.6x at P48 and forward P/E of 22.3x, so I call it fair overall, not cheap. The main risks are muddy cash flow and earnings quality: finance costs jumped 85% YoY on acquisition-related borrowing, H1 FY26 earnings were weakly backed by cash (0.67x CFO/PAT, negative free cash flow), and analysts have trimmed next-year EPS estimates (−2.4% over 30 days, −3.7% over 90 days) even as they raised this year's.

fundamental.thesis: Linde India is a subsidiary of the global Linde group that makes industrial gases and also runs a lower-margin project engineering arm. Gases bring in about 71% of segment revenue at a 26.4% segment margin, while project engineering earns only 9.8%. The latest extracted quarter, Q1FY27, shows revenue of ₹694 cr, up 21.6% YoY, but PAT fell 2.4% YoY to ₹105 cr. PAT margin has slipped to 15.1% from the low-to-mid 20s in earlier periods, and the H1 EBITDA margin dropped 850 bps to 31.8%. In short, sales are growing faster but that growth is not reaching profit, and heavy capex (about 96% of H1 revenue) pushed free cash flow to -₹647 cr. Industrial gases is a utility-like business, not a steel or cement cyclical, so I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA and peer multiples. EV/EBITDA was not available, so I fell back on peer multiples: trailing P/E of 99.6x, forward P/E of 73.8x and P/B of 12.7x put it at P93/P98/P89 against the broad market, roughly 180-220% above the median, which is clearly expensive. Sell-side next-year EPS estimates have been cut about 14% over the last 30-90 days. The Q2FY27 results (filed 3 Nov) have not been extracted yet, so this view rests on Q1 and H1 data.

fundamental.thesis: Narayana Hrudayalaya runs a large chain of affordable multi-specialty and cardiac hospitals in India and also owns a hospital business in the UK, which makes it a mid-sized hospital operator that grows by adding beds and raising occupancy and revenue per bed. PAT is the cleanest figure we have: Q2FY27 PAT was ₹301 cr, up 16.7% YoY (EPS ₹14.82 vs ₹12.72), faster than Q1FY27's +5.4%. Revenue figures disagree with each other, though: the filings table shows ₹2,896 cr (+73.6% YoY) while yfinance shows ₹1,627 cr, and the prior-year comparison rows look mis-scaled. Margins are clearly falling either way (operating margin down about 500 bps to 19.5%, H1 EBITDA margin 20.1% vs 25.0%), and strong cash conversion (H1 CFO/PAT 1.91x, FCF ₹594 cr) is the main support. Using EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-heavy hospital chain, the stock trades at 25.4x, which is at or below where Indian hospital peers usually trade. Trailing P/E is 46.9x, but forward P/E of 26.6x implies earnings growth ahead, and the stock sits at 36% of its 52-week range, so fair overall. The biggest risk is that margins keep shrinking while debt stays high (D/E about 1.2x) and analysts have cut FY EPS estimates by 3.7% over 30 days even though almost all of them rate it a buy.

fundamental.thesis: Neuland Laboratories makes APIs (active drug ingredients) and does contract development and manufacturing (CDMO) for global drugmakers. About 85% of revenue comes from exports, and it has 77 active US drug master files (DMFs) and a clean FDA record. It should benefit from the China+1 shift, and its export-led model is outside the US tariff on patented drugs. Results are lumpy, though: Q2FY27 revenue fell 11.4% YoY to ₹457 cr and PAT fell 47% to ₹51 cr. That came straight after an exceptional Q1 (revenue +116%, PAT ₹147 cr), and the PAT margin dropped from 22.7% to 11.2% between the two quarters. H1FY27 still looks strong, with revenue up 35% to ₹1,091 cr, PAT up 80% to ₹199 cr and cash flow from operations at 1.8x PAT. On valuation I used trailing and forward P/E and P/B, because the reported EV/EBITDA of 401x and debt/equity of 16x are almost certainly data errors for a company the filings show as net cash. At 60.6x trailing earnings (sector range 28–40x), 11.8x book and the P78 peer percentile, the stock is expensive. The 37.6x forward P/E already assumes the H1 growth rate carries on. The biggest risk is that the Q2 drop marks a pause in big customer orders rather than normal quarter-to-quarter swings, which would leave a premium valuation without the earnings to support it.

H1 FY27 revenue fell 12.4% YoY to ₹2,060 cr (from ₹2,352 cr), and EBITDA fell 27% to ₹101 cr, with margin down from 6.2% to 4.9%. Reported PAT of ₹530 cr (attributable ₹476 cr, up 3,001% YoY) comes almost entirely from a one-off current-tax credit of about ₹557 cr: before tax the company lost ₹27 cr, operating cash flow covered only 0.21× of PAT, and revenue growth has fallen from +11.4% to the negative range over the trend window. P/E (36.8×, in line with the market median) and EV/EBITDA (negative) are both distorted by the tax credit and the weak EBITDA, so I graded on P/B plus ROE: 1.42× book is low for the broad market (P9) but matches a 3% ROE, so fair, not cheap; on underlying earnings the stock is effectively loss-making, and the price sitting near its 52-week low (10% of range) looks more like a falling knife than value. The biggest risk is leverage: net debt is ₹1,471 cr, about 7.3× annualised EBITDA, and the promoter pledged more shares again in October and November 2026.

TBO Tek runs a B2B travel-distribution platform that connects travel agents worldwide to hotel and airline inventory, and since the Classic Vacations acquisition it also has a North American leisure arm. In Q2FY27 reported revenue of ₹866 cr grew 52.5% YoY, slower than Q1's +81%, and most of that headline growth comes from the acquisition: organic GTV grew 22% and organic gross profit 21%, while organic adjusted EBITDA grew 36%. Consolidated EBITDA margin has contracted from 22.5% to 17.6% over the trend window, and the last PAT margin we have is 9.0% in Q1FY27, down from about 14% a year earlier, because the lower-margin Classic Vacations business now makes up more of the mix. Q2 PAT was not available from the filings, and the revenue scale in the trend table does not match the yfinance rows, so treat the absolute figures with some caution. On valuation, the sector card says platform names should be judged on EV/EBITDA and growth delivery, not P/E alone: at 39.3x EV/EBITDA (P81 vs the broad market) and 68.4x trailing P/E (P83), with the stock at 88.8% of its 52-week range, the shares look expensive even though the forward P/E of 33.5x assumes strong earnings growth. The biggest risk is that the price assumes perfection while FY EPS estimates were cut about 10% in the last 30 days and governance issues are piling up: an unprovisioned ED/FEMA penalty of about ₹22 cr, an ₹8.1 cr employee fraud at an overseas subsidiary, and ₹8.9 cr of FX losses.

Latent View Analytics is a mid-cap data-analytics and AI consulting firm with about 1,800 employees and 40 Fortune 500 clients; it is still growing much faster than tier-1 Indian IT, which is close to flat. Growth is slowing quarter by quarter, though. Revenue growth fell from +27.3% YoY in H1FY26 and +24.3% in FY26 to +14.2% in Q2FY27 (₹294 cr). Q2 PAT was ₹48 cr (+6.1% YoY), and H1FY27 PAT was flat at -0.8% even though revenue grew 17.7%. Margins are shrinking because employee costs rose 21.8% YoY and now take 68.8% of revenue, and outside Industrials (+21.4%) the segments are barely growing (Financial Services +3.5%, CPG/Retail +2.7%). On valuation I used the IT sector P/E range plus EV/EBITDA. Trailing P/E is 32.3x, a little above the 22–30x IT range. Forward P/E is 22.1x and EV/EBITDA is 24.2x, close to the broad-market median (about P50). That makes it fair overall, not cheap, since estimates are being cut. The biggest worry is earnings quality: in H1 only about 26% of profit turned into operating cash (CFO/PAT 0.26x, down from 0.60x), and analysts have cut FY EPS estimates by 6% over 90 days. Both suggest the growth premium could shrink further.

fundamental.thesis: Nava is a diversified midcap that earns money from a coal-fired power plant and coal mining in Zambia (MEL), merchant and captive thermal power in India, and ferro-alloy (silico-manganese) production in Odisha. It is a power-and-metals cyclical, not a regulated utility like NTPC or POWERGRID. In Q1FY27, consolidated revenue was ₹1,212 cr, up only 1.6% YoY. PAT was ₹333 cr, down 16.6% YoY from ₹399 cr, and EBITDA fell 7.0% YoY to ₹584 cr. Revenue growth has slowed from +20.9% in Q3FY26 to +7.7% for FY26 and +1.6% now. The big QoQ jump (PAT +144%) mostly recovers from a weak Q4, helped by higher plant load factors (India 85.4%, Zambia 89.3%), and does not mark a new uptrend. Cash conversion is a real positive: operating cash flow was 2.9x PAT in FY26, with ₹505 cr of free cash flow. I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA because this is a capital-intensive business. At 10.0x EV/EBITDA, 1.79x P/B and 20.9x trailing P/E, the stock sits in the bottom quartile of the broad market (P10 on EV/EBITDA, P14 on P/B), but its P/E is above the 10–18x utilities band. Once you allow for Zambia country risk and cyclical earnings, I'd call it fair rather than clearly cheap. The near-term risks are the Q2FY27 results on 12 Nov 2026, the Odisha 60MW plant shutdown in September, and the 300MW MEL Phase 2 delay to mid-2028, which pushes out the next growth step.

GMDCLTD is a Gujarat state-owned miner whose main business is lignite. Mining brings in nearly all its revenue (FY26 mining revenue ₹2,508 cr out of ₹2,653 cr total), and the loss-making power segment adds the rest. In Q2FY27, revenue from the official filing rose 71.2% YoY to ₹903 cr, faster than +23.8% in Q1FY27. Reported PAT fell 63.3% to ₹171 cr, but that is because Q2FY26 included a one-time ₹474 cr GST credit; without it, PAT grew about 27%. The PAT margin is 18.9%, close to Q1's 18.0% and well below FY26's 36% (which was inflated by the one-off). The quarter was strongly cash-backed: operating cash flow was 3.9x PAT and free cash flow ₹376 cr. Because this is a capital-heavy commodity miner, the right measure is EV/EBITDA, and the reported 43.9x is far above the 5–8x mid-cycle norm for cyclicals. However, that figure, the 163% dividend yield and the 4.47 debt/equity do not fit with Q1 EBITDA of ₹267 cr and the low liabilities in the segment data, so I treat them as unreliable. On the more dependable cross-check, trailing P/E of 20.6x is at the top of the 12–22x Materials range and P/B of 2.78x with 14.2% ROE is not cheap. Forward P/E (22.0x) is above trailing, which means earnings are expected to fall, so the grade is fair, not cheap, even though the stock ranks low on P/E against the broad market. The biggest risk is that the 71% revenue jump does not match the yfinance figure (₹538 cr), and it brought only modest underlying profit growth while margins shrank.

At 17.1x EV/EBITDA, 30.1x trailing P/E (above the 12–22x Materials range) and 2.6x book for only a 9% ROE, the stock is priced for a margin recovery the filings don't yet show. Forward P/E of 28.7x is barely below trailing. The broad-market peer ranks (P31 on EV/EBITDA) compare it with unrelated sectors, so I gave them little weight. The stock trades near its 52-week low, but that alone is not a reason to buy.

fundamental.thesis: CEAT is India's #4 tyre maker (global rank #4 by brand) with 51% replacement, 30% OEM, and 19% export mix, operating at 95% capacity utilisation across ~80,000 daily tyres — a capital-intensive ancillary with defensive replacement demand. The single biggest risk is that commodity costs (natural rubber, crude derivatives) persist or worsen into H2FY27, keeping EBITDA margins pinned at 9–10% and preventing the earnings recovery the forward P/E demands — a second consecutive quarter of PAT decline would trigger a meaningful derating.

On valuation it looks cheap: trailing P/E is 12.6x against an IT sector band of 22–30x, EV/EBITDA is 8.2x (P7 across the market), and forward P/E of 11.2x is below trailing. Brainbees (FirstCry) is India's largest multi-channel retailer for baby and kids products, with GlobalBees brand roll-ups, an international arm and preschools on the side. Profitability is getting worse: adjusted EBITDA was flat YoY, India multi-channel EBITDA margin fell 290 bps, and the gross margin is still 260 bps short of where it was. The data for profit is unreliable: the trend table shows PAT of ₹51 cr (+34%), while yfinance shows a loss of ₹31 cr on revenue of ₹1,337 cr, and the filings index says its latest extracted results are from H1 FY26, so I am not relying on any PAT figure. The sector card says to judge loss-making platforms like this one on EV/sales, growth and unit economics, not P/E. On that basis the stock is fair rather than cheap: price/sales of 1.24x and P/B of 2.18x are low for a platform, but EV/EBITDA of 159x (most expensive in its peer set) and a forward P/E of 49x mean you are paying for a margin recovery that hasn't happened yet. The biggest risk is that Q2 results on 14 Nov show the promised gross-margin recovery not arriving, as quick-commerce and pharmacy competitors keep pressuring diapers (about 15% of GMV).

fundamental.thesis: Gabriel India is a domestic auto-component maker focused on shock absorbers and suspension. It leads in commercial vehicles (about 88% market share) and electric two-wheelers (about 57%), and about 40% of revenue comes from the replacement/aftermarket business. H1 FY27 revenue grew 20.8% YoY to Rs 2,673 cr, speeding up from +15.5% in Q1 FY27 and +14.8% for FY26. That leaves an implied Q2 of about Rs 1,247 cr. Profits are not keeping up: PBT grew only about 10% YoY, Q1 FY27 EBITDA margin was 8.7% against 9.6% in FY26, and the restatement after the demerger plus the new stakes in HL Mando Anand and HL Klemove make the growth partly inorganic and harder to compare year on year. Valuation is expensive however you measure it. The trailing P/E of 65x is far above the 18-28x auto band. EV/EBITDA of 36.9x (the main yardstick here, since the business is shifting toward a capital- and acquisition-heavy holding structure) and P/B of 12x sit in the top quartile of the broad market (P77 and P88). The forward P/E of 31.8x and recent FY EPS upgrades (+6.2% over 30 days) already assume strong earnings growth, while next-year estimates are edging down (-1.2% over 30 days). The biggest risk is that the deals take net debt from about Rs 2 cr to Rs 1,125 cr while operating cash flow falls 36% YoY, so any slip in integration or margins hits a stock priced for perfection.

fundamental.thesis: Jaiprakash Power Ventures is a midcap private power producer (thermal plus the Vishnu Prayag hydro plant) whose former promoter group, Jaiprakash Associates, was taken over by Adani Enterprises through insolvency in March 2026; it does not fit the regulated-return model the Utilities sector card describes. That jump follows a weak FY26 (revenue +1.9%, PAT -44.6%) and is distorted by a one-time ₹108 cr net tax benefit and a ₹194 cr coal-mine surrender provision. The Q2 FY27 results filed on 19 Oct are not yet in the trend table, and the unverified yfinance figures (PAT ₹33 cr) hint at a sharp seasonal or underlying drop, so the 'accelerating' trajectory label should not be trusted. Using EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick for this capital-heavy business, 11.4x (P16 vs the broad market) and P/B of 1.23x look reasonable, but trailing P/E of 22.9x is above the 10–18x utilities band, so overall it is fair, not cheap. fundamental.thesis: HINDPETRO is a state-run oil marketing and refining company whose earnings depend mainly on the gap between crude costs and government-influenced retail fuel and LPG prices. Q2FY27 revenue was about ₹1,39,213 cr (H1 ₹2,84,339 cr minus Q1 ₹1,45,126 cr), up roughly 26% YoY from ₹1,10,323 cr, but this growth comes from higher prices rather than profit: Q2 PAT recovered to ₹3,625 cr (2.6% margin, partly helped by ₹3,960 cr of H1 LPG compensation) after a Q1 loss of ₹12,265 cr, leaving H1 at a ₹8,639 cr loss and H1 EBITDA margin at -1.9% versus about 6.7% a year earlier. Using P/E plus dividend yield and EV/EBITDA, the yardstick the sector card sets for OMCs, the headline 4.7x trailing P/E and 4.2x EV/EBITDA look like the cheapest in the market, but they are stale: they reflect FY26 PAT of ₹18,047 cr, while actual trailing-four-quarter PAT is only about ₹1,200 cr (roughly 70x). The 7.3x forward P/E is therefore better read as policy-priced and fair, not cheap. The biggest risk is crude above $100 with a weakening rupee: marketing losses could return while the balance sheet is already stretched, with short-term borrowings up to ₹35,933 cr, a current ratio of 0.57, negative interest coverage and an ₹18,049 cr unrecognised LPG under-recovery.

IGL is the main city gas distributor in Delhi NCR, selling CNG to vehicles and piped gas (PNG) to homes and businesses. It is still adding volume: total volumes grew 6.9% YoY to 9.86 MMSCMD in H1 FY27, CNG rose 7.5% and domestic PNG rose 11.5%. Profits, however, have collapsed. H1 FY27 revenue grew 21.4% to ₹10,654 cr, but gas purchase costs jumped 39%, EBITDA margin fell from 12% to 3%, and PAT dropped 71% to ₹211 cr (a 2.0% margin). Q2 alone was much worse: EBITDA was negative ₹31 cr and PAT was about ₹26 cr, down roughly 93% from ₹386 cr a year earlier. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA and P/E, as suits a capital-intensive utility. On those, the stock looks cheap: trailing P/E is 15.4x (inside the 10–18x utilities range), EV/EBITDA is 10.5x and the stock sits around the 12th–15th percentile of the market. But both figures are based on trailing earnings that are falling fast, and analysts have cut current-year EPS estimates by 50–59% in 90 days. So I grade it fair, and the low multiples may be a value trap. The biggest risk is that IGL cannot raise CNG and PNG prices to cover higher gas costs (in a politically sensitive Delhi market, with crude near $91 and rising), so margins stay crushed.

fundamental.thesis: Reliance Power is a midcap private generator with about 5.3 GW operating, mostly coal (Sasan ultra-mega plant with a long-term contract, running at about 92% load factor, plus Rosa). Only 145 MW is renewable, and another 4.8 GW of renewable and hydro capacity is stuck in the pipeline. In Q1 FY27 consolidated revenue grew 3.8% YoY to ₹1,956 cr and PAT rose 44.9% YoY to ₹65 cr, a thin 3.3% PAT margin. This follows a FY26 loss of ₹337 cr, which came after a ₹38,160 cr asset write-down. The 'accelerating' revenue signal is mostly noise across quarters: growth has gone +12.2%, ~+1.5%, +0.5%, +3.8%, so the real picture is low-single-digit growth with no management guidance. I used EV/EBITDA, the right measure for a capital-heavy power company, plus P/B. At 8.3x EV/EBITDA (P8 vs the broad market) and 0.69x book, the stock looks cheap. But ROE is negative at -2.1% and interest costs eat about 18% of revenue, so a large part of the discount is a fair price for balance-sheet and governance risk, not a clear mispricing. The biggest risk is group solvency: auditors have flagged going-concern doubts, subsidiary RSTEPL has defaulted on about ₹2,296 cr of debt, and lenders have called a parent guarantee of about ₹1,842 cr for SMPL, which is now in insolvency proceedings. Any of these could wipe out the equity value that the low P/B seems to offer.

rules.eligible: growth == strong, risk != high, data_quality != poor, revenue growth not decelerating (newest results period's YoY revenue growth >= the preceding period's, from the filing extracts; a missing number passes)
rules.rank: revenue acceleration (highest first), then revenue growth, then symbol
rules.entry: next open, once the newest results filing is >= 5 sessions old; skipped when up > 5% over 5 sessions; slots freed by sells are refilled from the eligible list the same session
rules.hold: re-judged every session on the latest view (refreshed on each results filing); topped up toward target when below 75% of target and cash allows (anti-chase applies; entries are funded first); re-qualification review every 120 sessions since entry (then since the last review): must still pass growth == strong, risk != high, revenue growth not decelerating (a missing number passes), else sold — a name failing the gate but not deteriorated is sold only at this review, never earlier
rules.exit: growth -> weak, risk -> high, sentiment bearish with conviction >= 0.5, or the 120-session review failing (growth not strong, risk high or decelerating); between reviews never for decelerating, never for timing, never on missing data

books.hypothesis: The pre-c1 Book 3 — moderate growers and the conviction leg, no acceleration leg — run live beside Book 3 to settle c1 vs (a) out of sample (the first 98-session replay had (a) ahead).

rules.eligible: growth in {strong, moderate}, risk != high, data_quality != poor, conviction >= 0.5 (fundamental_filter_v1, the original rule (a))
rules.rank: growth grade (strong first), then conviction, then symbol
rules.entry: next open; skipped when up > 5% over 5 sessions (no results-timing leg); slots freed by sells are refilled the same session
rules.hold: re-judged every session on the latest view (refreshed on each results filing); topped up toward target when below 75% of target and cash allows (anti-chase applies; entries are funded first); re-qualification review every 120 sessions since entry (then since the last review): must still pass growth in {strong, moderate}, risk != high, conviction >= 0.5 (rule (a) without the data-quality leg), else sold — a name failing the gate but not deteriorated is sold only at this review, never earlier
rules.exit: growth -> weak, risk -> high, sentiment bearish with conviction >= 0.5, or the 120-session review failing (rule (a) no longer met); between reviews never for decelerating, never for timing, never on missing data
rules.overlay: target exposure 1.0 above / 0.5 below the equal-weight large-cap proxy's 200-day SMA (state confirmed over 5 consecutive sessions), applied to the whole book: every target weight is exposure/N and holdings are rebalanced toward it on the session the state flips (band +/-25%); this book trims on the flip down and tops up any session
rules.review_gate: growth in {strong, moderate}, risk != high, conviction >= 0.5

books.title: Book 6 bottom-up, neutral tilts (no model)
books.hypothesis: Book 6's construction with every sector tilt at 1.0, run live beside Book 6: the line the model tilt must beat by more than the random band (the bounds study of 26 Oct 2026 found no pack field beat it; the TWR line cannot judge the tilt, Book 6 − b6_neutral and the sector-call scorecard can).

rules.signal: monthly signal date recorded (rebalance cadence); NO sector_strategist call
rules.tilt: 1.0 for every sector, always (neutral = equal share over the sectors with eligible names or a holding)
rules.eligible: the shared fundamental filter: growth == strong, risk != high, data_quality != poor, revenue growth not decelerating (newest results period's YoY revenue growth >= the preceding period's, from the filing extracts; a missing number passes); ranked by revenue acceleration (highest first), then revenue growth, then symbol
rules.slots: 30 slots apportioned over the active sectors by largest remainder on w_s x 30 (sum = 30 exactly), with hysteresis: a sector's count changes only when its exact share moves > 0.5 slot from its current allocation; weight w_s / k_s each, capped at 2/30
rules.overlay: target exposure 1.0 above / 0.5 below the equal-weight large-cap proxy's 200-day SMA (state confirmed over 5 consecutive sessions), applied to the whole book: every target weight is exposure/N and holdings are rebalanced toward it on the session the state flips (band +/-25%); rebalanced on the monthly signal date and on the flip
rules.entry: next open, once the newest results filing is >= 5 sessions old; skipped when up > 5% over 5 sessions or exited in the last 20 sessions
rules.exit: fundamental deterioration (growth -> weak / risk -> high), or a tilt cut dropping k_s below the names held (lowest-ranked sold first); never on missing data, decelerating growth or timing
rules.rebalance: signal dates and the session the overlay flips; survivors outside +/-25% of target
rules.attribution: monthly Brinson vs the equal-weight universe (leaderboard key b6_neutral_attribution); no sector calls, so no scorecard
rules.judge: the comparator for Book 6: Book 6 − b6_neutral is the tilt's contribution

books.title: Growth screen (ranked by PAT growth)
books.hypothesis: Avoid what the grades call losers (high risk, weak growth, poor data, decelerating), then buy the highest reported revenue growth — the one fundamental the winners forensic found on the winners' side — with Book 3's construction.

rules.eligible: risk != high, growth != weak, data_quality != poor, revenue growth not decelerating (a missing number passes), revenue growth YoY > 0 (newest results period with a number; missing fails)
rules.rank: PAT growth YoY from the filings, highest first (missing last), then revenue growth, then symbol
rules.entry: next open, once the newest results filing is >= 5 sessions old; skipped when up > 5% over 5 sessions; slots freed by sells are refilled from the eligible list the same session
rules.hold: re-judged every session on the latest view (refreshed on each results filing); topped up toward target when below 75% of target and cash allows (anti-chase applies; entries are funded first); re-qualification review every 120 sessions since entry (then since the last review): must still pass the same filter, else sold — a name failing the gate but not deteriorated is sold only at this review, never earlier
rules.exit: growth -> weak, risk -> high, or the 120-session review failing (the same filter); no sentiment exit
rules.overlay: target exposure 1.0 above / 0.5 below the equal-weight large-cap proxy's 200-day SMA (state confirmed over 5 consecutive sessions), applied to the whole book: every target weight is exposure/N and holdings are rebalanced toward it on the session the state flips (band +/-25%); this book trims on the flip down and tops up any session
rules.review_gate: risk != high, growth != weak, data_quality != poor, revenue growth not decelerating (a missing number passes), revenue growth YoY > 0 (newest results period with a number; missing fails)

books.kill_rule: more than 10 points behind the equal-weight null on a rolling 60-date basis, twice in a row
books.promote_rule: best book at 90 dates, if ahead of both benchmarks

brinson.method: Brinson-Fachler vs the equal-weight universe, start-of-month holdings held through the month; Cash is a sector with zero return and zero benchmark weight
